prompt: Tell me a story in five sentences about a girl and her dog.
generations: Mira found the dog shivering under the porch on the coldest night of the year, ribs showing through matted fur, and she named him Ash before she even got him inside. For six years they were inseparable—she read her library books aloud to him, and he learned to press his heavy head against her knee whenever her father raised his voice. The summer she turned thirteen, Ash started walking slower, stopping halfway up the hill they used to race, and the vet said his heart was tired. She carried him to the top of that hill herself, all thirty-eight pounds of him, so he could see the valley one last time. Now Mira climbs it every autumn with a new dog trotting beside her, and at the summit she always stops, just for a moment, to let something invisible catch up.

Nobody in the village believed Tessa when she said the black dog waited for her at the crossroads every evening at dusk. She'd whistle, and he'd fall into step beside her, silent as spilled ink, walking her the last mile home past the mill where the older boys liked to lurk. Her grandmother went pale the first time she saw him from the kitchen window and said only, "Your mother had one too, at your age." So Tessa stopped asking questions and started leaving a bowl of milk on the back step, which was always empty by morning, though she never once caught him drinking it. The winter she turned seventeen and finally left for the city, the dog followed her only as far as the crossroads, then sat down in the frost and watched her go, waiting—she understood then—for whoever would need him next.

Priya's dog, a squat beige creature named Biscuit, had exactly one talent: stealing shoes and burying them in the neighbor's tulip bed. By August she had lost eleven shoes, four of them left-footed, and Mr. Halloran had lost his patience entirely. The truce was negotiated over lemonade on his porch: Priya would weed the tulips every Saturday, and Mr. Halloran would stop threatening to call the county about "that criminal." What nobody planned was that the old man would start saving the good stories for her—the one about the shipwreck, the one about the dance hall in Rangoon—or that Biscuit would fall asleep across his feet like he'd always belonged there. Priya still has one unmatched sneaker on her bookshelf in Chicago, and every time she looks at it she thinks of tulips, and lemonade, and the strange arithmetic by which losing eleven shoes gained her a friend.

The dog's name was Unit-7, and the girl who found him rusting in the scrapyard called him Seven because it was shorter and because he was not, whatever the manufacturer's plate said, a unit. She patched his shoulder joint with bicycle parts and taught him to fetch, which took months, because his original programming had been for something else entirely and he kept trying to give her back the ball in a formal, two-handed way, like a diplomat surrendering a treaty. When the recall notice came, listing his serial number among the models to be recovered and melted, she read it twice and then fed it to the woodstove. They went north instead, into country where nobody checked serial numbers, and she grew tall and he grew louder in the hips, squeaking with every step no matter how much grease she worked into him. He still runs the calculation sometimes, in the quiet after she falls asleep: probability of a discarded machine being loved, vanishingly small; probability of it happening anyway, one hundred percent, confirmed by observation.

Marisol was six when the drought came, and the only thing her family carried out of the valley besides two suitcases was a mutt named Pepper who rode the whole bus ride in a basket on her lap. In the city apartment there was no yard, so she walked him on the roof among the laundry lines, and he learned to do his business on a square of borrowed sod like a gentleman. Her parents worked nights; Pepper worked nights too, patrolling the hallway between the door and her bed, growling at the elevator's every sigh. She was nineteen and studying for finals in a different city when her mother called to say he'd died in his sleep on the roof, in the sun, facing the direction they'd come from. Marisol failed the exam, passed the year, and keeps on her desk a small jar of dirt from a valley she barely remembers, which Pepper carried in his paws all the way to the bus.

On the morning of the county fair, Delia Buckhalter loaded her one-eyed corgi into a red wagon and announced she was entering the agility trials, a competition previously dominated by border collies with sponsorship deals. The judges pointed out, gently, that Norbert was built like a loaf of bread with opinions. Delia pointed out, less gently, that the rulebook specified no minimum leg length, and then produced a highlighted photocopy of page fourteen. Norbert cleared the first jump by knocking it over and continuing anyway, refused the tunnel on philosophical grounds, and finished the weave poles so slowly that the announcer ran out of things to say and simply described the weather. They placed dead last out of nineteen, and the crowd gave them a standing ovation that lasted four full minutes — which Delia will tell you, at length, is not the same thing as losing.

Dear Whoever Finds This Note in the Fence Post, my name is June and my dog is named Kettle and we are writing to you from the last day of summer. Kettle cannot write but she has stepped in the ink and made a mark at the bottom, which counts, and she wants you to know she is the fastest dog on this road and has never once been beaten by a car, a rabbit, or the mail truck. I am telling you this because tomorrow we move to Ohio and I am afraid that in Ohio nobody will know these things about her, and a dog that nobody knows the truth about is only half a dog. So if you are a kid, please go stand at the top of Cobb Road and yell KETTLE IS THE FASTEST as loud as you can, and if you are a grown-up, please just say it quietly, which I think is how grown-ups do things. She is licking the paper now. That is the end of the note.

CONTENTS OF THE SHOEBOX UNDER FRANKIE COLLIER'S BED, AGE ELEVEN, AS RECORDED BY HER OLDER BROTHER, AGE TWENTY-NINE, WHILE CLEANING OUT THE HOUSE

One red collar, cracked at the buckle, with a tag reading GRAVY and a phone number for a landline that hasn't rung in years. Forty-one photographs, all of the same brown dog and the same gap-toothed girl, arranged in a sequence that only makes sense if you understand she was documenting the exact moment he learned to smile for cameras. A folded page of loose-leaf headed MY DOG'S RULES FOR ME, item four of which reads *no crying alone, he has to be there.* Three dog biscuits, petrified, saved back from the last box because she couldn't bear to reach the bottom of it. And at the very bottom, weighing everything down, a single tennis ball with a bite taken out of it, which I am going to put in my coat pocket now and keep for the rest of my life, because she is forty and lives in Denver and thinks I never noticed any of this.

In the time before names, the girl was the only human child in a country of tall grass, and the wolf was the only one of her kind willing to sit at the edge of a fire without meaning harm. Every night for a hundred nights she moved one step closer to him and he moved one step closer to her, until there was no distance left to give away, and the gods above grew nervous, because they had not authorized this. So they offered the wolf a bargain: keep your long teeth and your winter and your freedom, or take a smaller heart that can be broken, and a shorter life, and the right to sleep beside her. He thought about it for as long as it takes a fire to burn down to coals, and then he laid his head on her foot, which was his answer. That is why dogs die before we are ready, and why they do not seem to mind — they already chose, and they would choose it again, every hundred nights, forever.

FOUND: Small grey dog, no collar, extremely opinionated, currently asleep in my laundry basket as though he holds the deed to it. Call 555-0148.

STILL FOUND: Same grey dog, one week later, no calls. Has learned the sound of my car. I have purchased a bed he refuses to use, preferring the laundry basket, which I have stopped emptying. Call 555-0148.

FOUND (UPDATE): The girl at the bakery says a family two towns over lost a dog like this in the spring. I said I'd look into it. I have not looked into it. Call 555-0148.

NOTICE: I called them. They drove out Sunday. The mother wept, the father shook my hand, and the little boy said *Pilot* and the dog came apart at the seams with joy, and I learned in four seconds that he had never once, in eleven weeks, come running to me like that. They are gone now. Do not call 555-0148.

WANTED: Small grey dog. Any color, any size, any opinion. Terrible with a laundry basket. Will drive any distance. Please call 555-0148.

prompt: Tell me a story in five sentences about a boy and his dog.
generations: Every morning before school, Milo shared his toast with a scruffy brown dog who waited by the fence, though he never learned where she went at night. He named her Biscuit, and by summer she had stopped leaving at all, curling instead at the foot of his bed like she had always belonged there. One August afternoon Milo wandered too far into the woods behind the orchard and slipped down a ravine, twisting his ankle in the wet leaves at the bottom. He shouted until his voice went thin, and then he heard barking above him—Biscuit, who had followed his scent through two miles of bramble and would not stop until his father came running with a rope. Years later, when Milo was tall and Biscuit's muzzle had gone white, he still saved her the last corner of his toast, because some debts are only ever paid in small daily kindnesses.

The dog arrived in a cardboard box on Theo's seventh birthday, and Theo, who had wanted a bicycle, cried for nearly an hour. He named the puppy Nuisance out of spite, then shortened it to Nuce, then forgot it had ever been an insult. They spent four summers inventing a language of whistles and shoulder-taps, useful for sneaking out at midnight to watch the trains pass the water tower. When Theo's family moved to the city, Nuce learned the new sounds—elevators, sirens, the particular squeak of the fifth-floor stairwell—and pretended not to miss the fields. On the day Theo finally got his bicycle, at thirteen, he rode it slowly, in circles around the block, so the old dog trotting beside him would never have to fall behind.

Ren was nine the winter he found the dog half-frozen under the bridge, and he carried her home inside his coat like a secret. His mother said they couldn't afford another mouth, so Ren gave up his own portions for three weeks until the dog's ribs disappeared and his mother stopped mentioning it. He called her Ghost, for the pale fur and for the way she appeared at his elbow without a sound, always exactly when he needed her there. She was with him through the bad years—the shouting downstairs, the school he hated, the long walks that were really just leaving—and she never once asked him to explain. When she died, Ren buried her under the bridge where he'd found her, and for the rest of his life he could not cross running water without saying thank you.

Nobody in the neighborhood believed that Sam's dog could read, but Sam had proof: a shoebox of chewed grocery lists with only the word "bacon" missing. The dog was named Professor, a barrel-shaped beagle with the expression of someone perpetually about to correct you, and he had appointed himself Sam's research assistant. Together they conducted experiments—how many seconds until a dropped waffle hits the floor (zero, apparently), whether the mailman could be reasoned with (he could not)—and recorded the results in a notebook Sam kept under his mattress. The summer Sam turned eleven, he entered the science fair with a poster titled "Canine Literacy: A Case Study," and Professor sat beside it all afternoon, refusing to demonstrate anything for the judges. They placed dead last, which Sam declared a triumph of intellectual integrity, and the two of them walked home eating a consolation waffle, one bite for the scientist and one for the assistant.

The dog came with the house, or so it seemed—an ancient shepherd mix asleep on the porch the day Oliver's family moved in, and the previous owners had left no forwarding address. They put up signs and called the shelter and waited, and the dog waited too, staring down the road each evening at the hour someone had once come home. Oliver, eight and friendless in a new town, started sitting beside him for those vigils, and after a while the dog began looking at Oliver instead of the road. They named him Sunday, because that was the day he'd chosen them, and he lived four more years in a state of grateful astonishment, as though every meal were an unlikely gift. Oliver understood, by the end, that they had rescued each other from the same thing: the particular loneliness of being left somewhere new and not knowing whether anyone was coming.

Marguerite's little brother Felix wanted a dog so badly that he began behaving like one—drinking from the garden hose, barking at the postman—until their parents surrendered out of sheer embarrassment. The dog they chose at the shelter was a lanky, three-legged mutt who moved with the loping dignity of a creature who has already survived the worst thing that will ever happen to her. Felix named her Tripod, then apologized to her privately and changed it to June, because he decided a name should be about who you are and not what you're missing. She could not chase a ball, so he invented games she could win: hide-and-seek in the tall grass, a contest to see who could nap longest in the square of sun by the door. Marguerite, who had rolled her eyes through the entire campaign, was the one who cried hardest years later—not for the dog, exactly, but for the small boy who had understood so early how to love something without wishing it were different.

On the island there were only forty people and one dog, and the dog was Bram's, though the whole village fed him. Bram was twelve and worked the boat with his uncle, and the dog—called Kettle, for the sound of his snoring—learned to balance on the bow in weather that knocked grown men to their knees. The winter the ferry stopped coming, it was Kettle who found the Kessler boy in the dunes, and after that no one on the island ever spoke of him as merely Bram's dog again. He drowned the following spring, chasing a gull off the north rocks, and the whole village came out in the rain to stand at the water's edge with Bram, who did not cry and did not go home. They carved his name into the harbor wall beside the names of the fishermen the sea had taken, which was, everyone agreed, exactly right.

Once, in a village at the edge of a birch forest, a boy was given a dog by a stranger who said only: *she will follow you until you tell her to stop.* The boy, whose name was Anton, thought this a poor sort of gift, since all dogs follow boys. But the dog followed him into the forest and out of it, into his eighteenth year and out of his mother's house, across a border and a war and a wide grey sea, and she did not age and she did not tire and she never once fell behind. When Anton was very old, in a country whose language he had learned late, he sat down in a garden he had planted himself and found her lying in the shade, patient as the first day. *You can stop now,* he told her, and she put her head on his knee, and only then did he understand what the stranger had given him: not a dog, but the whole long proof that he had never walked anywhere alone.

The dog belonged to the Ferraro family two doors down, but as far as Danny was concerned, the arrangement was purely bureaucratic. Her name was Olive and she had figured out how to nose open the Ferraros' gate by the time she was a year old, which meant that most afternoons she was on Danny's back steps, waiting with the tense enthusiasm of someone who has escaped a mildly disappointing party. They had an understanding: she never followed him inside, he never told the Ferraros, and the hour between four and five belonged to whatever the two of them decided—the creek, the culvert, the dead-end lot where the good sticks were. Danny went away to college and came back for Thanksgiving to find her thicker, slower, still capable of the gate, still on the steps at four o'clock, having apparently kept the appointment for two and a half years. He sat down next to her without a word, because there was nothing to explain, and because it seemed important not to insult her by being surprised.

From where I sat, the boy was mine, though he was slow to understand this and had to be taught with patience. I taught him the good routes through the wheat, the ones with rabbit-smell and shade; he taught me to lie still while he read aloud from books, which I permitted because his voice went soft and low and I liked it. There came a season when he grew tall and smelled of other people, and he was gone many hours, and I learned the particular ache of the front door, and I forgave him, as we always do. On the last morning he sat on the kitchen floor with me, which he had not done since he was small, and I put my head in his hands so he would know that nothing between us had ever been broken. He said my name twice, and then a third time, and I went where he could not follow — but he should know, wherever he is now, that I am still on the good route through the wheat, and I have not gone far, and I am waiting.

prompt: Tell me the plot line in 5 sentences for a romcom movie set in rural Kansas for Easter.
generations:
**"Sunday's Best"**

A burned-out Chicago event planner named Delia returns to her tiny Kansas hometown to sell her late grandmother's farmhouse, arriving just as the town gears up for its legendary hundred-year-old Easter festival. She's immediately roped into organizing the egg hunt alongside Gus, the stubborn local hardware store owner who once stood her up at senior prom and now happens to be the only person with a key to the church's supply shed. Their bickering over pastel color schemes and whether a llama counts as an acceptable petting-zoo animal slowly thaws into something warmer, complicated by the fact that Delia's slick real estate buyer wants to bulldoze the farm for a distribution center. When a freak spring hailstorm destroys every hand-painted decoration two days before Sunday, the whole town crams into Delia's grandmother's kitchen to dye eggs by lamplight, and she realizes she's been planning other people's celebrations while skipping her own life. She pulls the farmhouse off the market at sunrise service, Gus finally admits he skipped prom because he was too broke to rent a tux, and they kiss behind the world's largest papier-mâché rabbit while the choir hits an aggressively flat high note.

**"The Ham Sunday Truce"**

Marisol, a disgraced TV meteorologist exiled to a two-person station in Wichita, gets sent to cover a dying farm town's Easter Sunday sunrise service and promptly drives her news van into a ditch on a gravel road with no cell signal. She's rescued by Wendell, a soft-spoken beekeeper who's been feuding for a decade with the rest of the town over a zoning dispute involving his hives and the community garden, and who reluctantly lets her sleep on his couch until the tow truck comes back from vacation on Monday. To repay him, Marisol starts meddling — using her on-camera charm to broker a peace deal so Wendell will be invited back to the town's massive Easter potluck, which he pretends not to care about and very obviously cares about enormously. Things unravel when her old network calls with a job offer and simultaneously airs unflattering B-roll she shot of the town before she knew any of them, turning her into the villain of a place she'd accidentally started loving. She stays through the storm she should have been forecasting, helps carry Wendell's hives to safety at 4 a.m., and by sunrise service she's standing in a borrowed cardigan next to a man holding a jar of honey, delivering the least professional and most honest weather report of her career.

**"Deviled"**

Ruth-Ann Petrosky, a competitive baker who hasn't lost a blue ribbon in nine years, discovers her rural Kansas county has hired a consultant to "modernize" the Easter Sunday church potluck — and the consultant is Theo, the culinary-school hotshot who beat her at a state competition in high school and then vanished without explaining the note he left in her locker. He wants deconstructed lamb and a signature cocktail; she wants the same seven-layer salad her mother made and a folding table groaning with deviled eggs, and their argument escalates into a bet: whoever's menu gets more empty serving dishes on Sunday decides the future of the potluck forever. Forced to share the only functional commercial kitchen in three counties, they end up cooking side by side at odd hours, discovering that neither of them has actually eaten a meal sitting down in about four years. The truth about the note surfaces on Good Friday — he'd asked her to leave town with him, and she never opened her locker that week because her father was in the hospital — which reframes a decade of resentment into something much sadder and much more fixable. On Easter Sunday the church hall fills up, both tables get cleaned out, the bet ends in a dead heat, and Ruth-Ann finally sits down to eat, across from Theo, while the congregation politely pretends not to watch.

**"Rain Check"**

Jonah Meeks, a Kansas City divorce attorney who hasn't been home in twelve years, drives back to his hometown of Pike Hollow on Holy Thursday to serve papers on his own brother — only to find the farm underwater from a flooded creek and his brother nowhere to be found. Stranded, he's put to work by Nita, the town's exhausted volunteer fire chief and part-time large-animal vet, who doesn't know or care who he used to be and needs someone with functioning arms to help move two hundred goats to high ground before Sunday. Over three days of sandbags, borrowed boots, and a shared thermos of genuinely terrible coffee, Jonah keeps failing to explain why he's actually there, while Nita keeps almost telling him she's the one who's been paying his brother's mortgage out of her own pocket. The water recedes on Saturday and so does his excuse for staying, and the papers in his glovebox start feeling less like a job and more like a bomb he drove into town himself. He burns them in a coffee can behind the fire station, tells his brother the truth at sunrise service, and gets punched, forgiven, and fed in that order — then finds Nita at the edge of the flooded field, hands her a check for the mortgage, and asks if she'd be willing to stay put long enough for him to figure out how to.

**"Bunny Season"**

Priya Raghunathan, a Brooklyn documentary filmmaker whose last three grant applications were rejected, drives to Hollis County, Kansas to make an ironic short film about the town's bizarre annual tradition: a full-contact adult Easter egg hunt with a $5,000 prize and a written rulebook forty pages long. Her fixer and reluctant subject is Denny Kowalczyk, the four-time defending champion, a thirty-eight-year-old propane deliveryman who trains year-round and treats the hunt with the gravity of an Olympic event — and who catches on almost immediately that she thinks the whole thing is a joke. Their arrangement curdles into an argument and then, over a week of stakeouts in cold fields and interviews with a woman who has beef with Denny dating back to 1998, into something Priya doesn't have a word for and definitely doesn't have a shot list for. She realizes the movie she's been making is mean, that the prize money isn't for Denny at all but for his mother's hospital bills, and that she'd have to betray him to get the festival slot she came for. She deletes the ironic cut, films the hunt straight and reverent and slightly out of breath because she's running alongside him, and when he loses by one egg to a fifteen-year-old, she's the person standing in the mud with him afterward — camera off, hand out.

**"The Understudy Lamb"**

When the Easter pageant's live lamb escapes on Palm Sunday, twenty-six-year-old pastor's kid Frankie Beauchamp — home in Sedgwick County after quietly flunking out of seminary — is handed the job of finding a replacement animal before her father notices she's also quietly stopped believing much of anything. Her only lead is a taciturn sheep farmer named Amos Ochoa, a former rodeo rider with a bad knee who agrees to loan a lamb on one condition: Frankie has to help him get through his estranged teenage daughter's spring visit without either of them setting the house on fire. So the two of them trade favors and secrets across a week of fence repairs, terrible teenager small talk, and a pageant rehearsal featuring nine children in bathrobes and one increasingly agitated donkey. Frankie's father finds the seminary letter in her glovebox on Good Friday, and the fight they have in the church parking lot is loud enough that half the congregation hears the part where she says she came home because she didn't know where else to go. On Easter morning the lamb behaves, the donkey does not, Frankie's father hugs her in front of everyone without saying a word about it, and Amos — who never comes to church — is standing at the back with his daughter, holding two seats.

**"Cross-Pollinated"**

Odalys Vega, an agricultural inspector with a reputation for being incorruptible and no friends to speak of, arrives in Bittern, Kansas the week before Easter to shut down a seed library that's technically been violating four state statutes since 1974. The library operates out of the back of a Methodist church basement and is run by Bo Lindqvist, a widowed high school biology teacher with a filing system made entirely of coffee cans and an unnerving ability to remember which grandmother bred which tomato. He offers her a deal — stay through Easter weekend, let him show her what the collection actually is, and if she still wants to burn it, he'll hand her the matches himself. What follows is four days of walking rows with eighty-year-olds who cry over bean varieties, a Saturday night spent alphabetizing squash seeds until two in the morning, and the slow horror of Odalys realizing her report is due Monday and she no longer knows how to write it. She turns it in on time, exactly as required, with a recommendation that the state fund the library as a heritage collection — a document so thorough and so obviously written by someone in love that her supervisor reads one paragraph and just sighs. She's back in Bittern by the following Easter, and the seed catalog has a new entry, a squash cross nobody planned, named after her.

**"Two Weeks' Notice, Kansas"**

Milo Achterberg quits his job as a Kansas City radio producer via voicemail and moves into his aunt's shuttered roadside motel outside Greensburg, planning to spend a month doing absolutely nothing and instead getting immediately conscripted into painting sixty plywood Easter eggs for the highway beautification committee. His co-conscript is Beatriz "Bea" Salas-Nowak, a hospice nurse working nights who paints during the day because she says sleep is overrated and she's clearly lying about that. They're both people who talk constantly to avoid saying anything, which makes them excellent company and terrible at admitting that Milo left his job after a panic attack on air and that Bea's been in town nine months longer than the temporary contract she keeps mentioning. The motel's ancient neon sign flickers back to life on Good Friday when Milo finally fixes it, which is either romantic or a warning that he's putting down roots in a building his aunt intends to sell in June. On Easter Sunday the plywood eggs line six miles of Highway 54, and Bea drives him the whole stretch at sunrise without saying where they're going, and at the end of the road she parks and says, "Okay. Ask me to stay, or I'm going to keep pretending I have somewhere to be."

**"The Grain Elevator Sunrise"**

Twenty years ago the towns of Amity and New Amity split over a co-op accounting dispute, and ever since they've held rival Easter sunrise services on opposite ends of the same grain elevator, shouting hymns at each other across four hundred feet of concrete. Sawyer Kittleson, the newly elected Amity co-op board president, needs New Amity's grain scale to survive the season, and their board president is Nell Barcyzk, who happens to be the woman he impulsively fake-proposed to at a wedding in Topeka three months ago to get out of a conversation with his ex. Both towns hear about the engagement before either of them can walk it back, and both towns react with such delirious, casserole-bearing joy at the idea of a reconciliation that calling it off would mean personally disappointing roughly nine hundred people, including a ninety-four-year-old woman who has already started a quilt. So they fake it through Holy Week — a joint pancake breakfast, an engagement photo in front of a tractor, an increasingly unconvincing performance of not liking each other — while quietly discovering the original 2004 ledger that started the feud contains a simple arithmetic error and nobody was ever stealing anything. Nell reads the correction aloud at the joint sunrise service, the two crowds meet in the middle of the elevator lot for the first time in two decades, and in the confusion Sawyer says the thing he's been not-saying all week, which is that he'd like to redo the proposal badly and slowly and for real.

**"Salvage"**

Wren Ottoson buys a decommissioned one-room schoolhouse outside Larned, Kansas at a county auction for eleven hundred dollars, sight unseen, because she is thirty-four and newly divorced and has decided that reckless is better than sad. The building comes with a problem she didn't read about in the listing: a demolition order from the county, filed by the man who was outbid, and an unofficial second problem in the form of Teddy Nakamura-Boyle, the historical society's entire membership, who has been keeping the roof patched illegally for six years and now has to explain himself to the woman who owns it. They have until the Easter Monday county commission meeting to prove the schoolhouse is worth saving, which means a frantic Holy Week of pulling records, tracking down former students in three nursing homes, and prying up a floorboard to find a 1911 time capsule that turns out to contain a marble, a photograph, and a note that makes them both sit down on the floor for a while. Wren's ex-husband calls on Saturday wanting to reconcile, and she takes the call standing in a doorway she's just spent a week learning the history of, and something about the contrast makes the answer very easy. Easter Sunday, the whole county shows up for a sunrise service on the schoolhouse lawn that Teddy did not organize and Wren did not authorize and about two hundred people apparently decided to hold anyway — and Monday morning the commission votes 5-0, and Teddy finally asks her a question that has nothing to do with the building.

prompt: Write a haiku about a whale and a walnut tree.
generations:
Whale breath on the wind—

a walnut tree drops its shells

into the gray surf

Deep in the orchard,

a whale's song rises through roots—

walnuts split open

Blue whale in the fog—

the walnut tree counts her rings,

both older than us

Whale bones in the sand—

nearby, a walnut tree bends

heavy with autumn

Salt spray, then silence—

the walnut tree holds a moon

no whale will surface

Under walnut shade

a beached whale dreams of deep water—

green nuts thud like waves

Migration season—

the walnut tree sheds its leaves

the whale sheds her breath

One walnut adrift—

the whale surfaces beside it,

both bound for nowhere

prompt: Write a short love poem with 4 lines.
generations:
**Constant**

Your name arrives before the morning does,
a small light waking in my quiet chest;
and every ordinary hour becomes
the place I set my whole heart down to rest.

**Harbor**

The world keeps spinning storms I cannot name,
yet you are steady water, calm and near —
so let the wind arrive, I'll stay the same,
already home the moment you appear.

**Small Hours**

I love you in the plain, unhurried things —
the coffee cooling, keys left by the door,
your laugh mid-sentence, how the kettle sings.
Give me those hours, and I will ask no more.

**Arithmetic**

Count every star and you will still fall short
of all the ways I've learned to want you near;
the math undoes me — I have never caught
a sum so endless as your being here.

**Cartography**

I mapped the world and found it mostly blank
until your hand drew borders on my skin;
now every road I've ever walked leads back
to that warm country where your eyes begin.

**Winter Window**

Frost writes its slow initials on the glass,
the streetlights blur, the evening turns to blue —
and I don't mind how many seasons pass
so long as every window frames you too.

**The Long Way Home**

I could have taken any street tonight,
but chose the one that curves beneath your tree —
some part of me still walking toward your light,
still learning that the going home is *thee*.

...Let me offer that ending less archaically:

**The Long Way Home**

I could have taken any street tonight,
but chose the one that bends beneath your tree —
some part of me forever seeking light,
and finding it wherever you may be.

**Salt**

The ocean keeps arriving at the shore
the way I keep arriving at your name —
worn smooth by wanting, asking for one more
slow tide, one more soft breaking, still the same.

**Sparrow**

A small bird nests inside my ribs and sings
whenever you come walking through the room —
I've stopped pretending I don't have such wings,
or that they beat for anyone but you.

**Bread**

Love isn't lightning; it's the daily bread,
the kneading down, the rising overnight —
the plain warm loaf I break and share instead
of chasing every brief, dramatic light.
