**Kept**

I keep you like a stone beneath my tongue,
smooth from the turning, bitter, never spat.
Some loves die clean. But you — you I have hung
in the cold cellar where I sharpen at.

**Rust**

You are the nail I hammered through my hand
to hold the door shut on a burning room.
I do not want you gone — I want you damned
and near, so I can watch you learn the smoke.

**Inheritance**

You gave me nothing but this iron taste,
and now it's mine — I've filed the edges bright.
Go on and rot; I'll keep the part you left,
the small cold hinge that lets me hate you right.

**Weather**

I don't want lightning. I want the long gray,
the drizzle that finds every seam you own,
the roof that gives an inch a year — and stays.
Let nothing strike you. Let you wear alone.

**Ledger**

I never burned your letters — that's for grief.
I filed them, dated, indexed, cross-referred.
I don't forgive, and I don't need relief;
I need the column where you owe, preserved.

**Guest**

I set your place each night and leave it cold —
one plate, one knife, no chair pushed in to meet it.
I built a house with one room you can't hold,
and I feed you nothing, nightly, just to keep it.

**Whetstone**

You think I've moved on. No — I've moved you in,
down where the grindstone turns and never tires.
Each year you're thinner and my edge more thin-
lipped bright. I'll thank you when the last spark fires.

**Root**

I pulled you up and found you'd gone too deep —
so now I garden round the thing you are.
Everything green here grows because I keep
you buried, feeding, hated, and not far.

**Salt**

I sowed the field between us, acre-wide,
so nothing grows to bridge it, ever, green.
Let no one call it healing when I stride
the white rows I keep barren, and keep clean.

**Clock**

I wound you into me and let you tick —
not love, not grief, just something keeping time.
Each hour you strike, I strike a match, and lick
the sulfur off, and call the hatred mine.

prompt: Write a short fable about a lemur and a light bulb.
generations:
**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

In a forest at the edge of a village, there lived a ring-tailed lemur named Bavo, who was famous among his troop for having the widest eyes and the longest leaps.

One night, Bavo spied a glow through the trees — a bare bulb burning above a farmer's doorway. It hung there without flickering, without smoking, steady as a small trapped sun.

"At last," said Bavo, "a moon that holds still."

He leapt from branch to fencepost to windowsill and seized the bulb in both hands. It burned him, and he fell, and the villagers' dogs chased him back into the dark.

His grandmother found him nursing his palms beneath a tamarind tree.

"You caught it, then," she said.

"I caught it," said Bavo, "and I learned nothing except that it is hot."

"You learned that it is hot," said the old lemur, "and that it does not want to be caught, and that the dogs are quick, and that your hands heal. That is four things. But you might have learned them at less cost by simply sitting here and *looking* at it."

Bavo turned his sore hands over. "Then why did no one tell me?"

"We did," said his grandmother. "But some creatures are built to hear a thing only after they have held it."

And Bavo went back many nights after, and sat, and watched the little steady sun — and found, to his surprise, that watching it was the better half of having it.

*Moral: What burns you teaches you; what you admire from a distance keeps you company longer.*

**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

A lemur named Zia lived in the crown of a baobab and believed, as all her family believed, that the stars were fireflies who had learned patience.

One dry season the villagers strung a wire between two poles, and at its center they hung a glass fruit. When the sun went down, the fruit turned gold.

Zia watched it for seven nights. On the eighth, she gathered the troop.

"I have found the seed of a star," she announced. "If we bring it home and bury it, our tree will grow stars of its own, and we will never be afraid of the dark again."

They stole it cleverly — Zia on the wire, two cousins below to catch it — and they buried the glass fruit in the good soil at the baobab's foot, and they waited.

It did not sprout. It did not shine. When the rains came, the water got in and the little coiled thread inside went soft and gray.

"It is dead," said Zia's cousin.

"It was never alive," said Zia. "That is the trouble. I saw only the light and thought that was the whole of the thing." She pressed the mud back over it. "But the light was the end of a long story, and I stole only the last word."

That night the troop sat in the dark and listened to the true fireflies, who were, after all, patient.

*Moral: A wonder torn from what sustains it is only a curiosity, and briefly at that.*

**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

A lemur crept into an empty research station and found a light bulb hanging from a cord.

"You are very bright," said the lemur.

"I am the brightest thing in this room," the bulb agreed.

"You are also very still. Don't you wish to go out into the forest?"

"Why should I? Everything worth seeing comes to *me*. The moths, the beetles, the little gray moon-eyed things — they all arrive at my feet and circle and praise me. In the forest I would have to look for things. Here, things look for me."

The lemur considered this, and being polite, said nothing, and went out into the night.

She saw the river carrying the sky on its back. She saw a chameleon change its mind three times. She saw a fig tree so heavy with fruit that it groaned, and she ate until she was sticky to the elbows, and she slept in a fork of the branches with her tail wrapped twice around her nose.

In the morning she passed the station again. The bulb was dark and silent, and beneath it lay a small drift of moths, each one perfect and still.

"Now you have your admirers forever," said the lemur, and went home.

*Moral: Beware the brilliance that never leaves its room — it gathers a crowd, but it does not gather a life.*

**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

An old lemur named Fitiavana was hired — or rather, appointed herself — as night watchman for a lodge at the forest's edge, where a single bulb burned on the veranda.

Every evening she took her post beside it and told the bulb the news: which fig trees were ripening, which hawk had moved her nest, which of her grandchildren had fallen out of a tree and pretended he'd meant to.

The bulb never answered. Fitiavana didn't mind. She had reached the age where the listening was the point.

One night a storm came through and knocked out the power for the whole valley. The lodge went black. The guests groped for candles and complained.

Fitiavana stayed on the veranda railing anyway. And she talked — about the storm, about the smell of the wet earth, about a lemur she had loved forty rains ago who had also been very quiet.

In the morning a young lemur asked her, "Why did you stay? The light was gone."

"Was it the light I was talking to?" said Fitiavana. "I thought it was myself. The bulb was only good manners."

*Moral: We often thank the lamp for the company we brought with us.*

**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

A mouse lemur, no bigger than a mango, took shelter inside a broken lantern one cold night and found himself nose to glass with a burnt-out bulb.

"Who are you?" asked the lemur.

"I *was* the light of this whole veranda," said the bulb. "Guests read by me. Lovers argued by me. A man once wept under me and thought no one saw. Then one evening I simply — stopped. Now I hang here, and they have not even troubled to throw me away."

"That is sad," said the lemur, and he curled up in the lantern's belly, because it was dry and out of the wind.

He came back the next night, and the next. Soon his mate came, and then there were four pink-eared babies asleep in the curve of the glass, and the bulb was the warmest thing in the garden by virtue of having six small bodies pressed against it.

"You should know," the bulb said one evening, "that I give no light at all now."

"I know," said the lemur, yawning. "We didn't come for the light. We came because you are shaped like a good place to be."

The bulb was quiet a long while.

"All those years," it said, "I thought that was the least interesting thing about me."

*Moral: When your purpose burns out, you may find you were always more than your purpose.*

**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

In a village at the forest's edge there was a single street lamp, and beneath it the lemurs held their councils, because under the lamp no owl could take them by surprise.

A clever young lemur named Rakoto noticed that the elders always sat closest to the pole.

"Why should the old have the brightest seats?" he asked. "Let us divide the light fairly. I propose we each take a turn directly beneath it."

The troop agreed, for it sounded just. So they took turns, each lemur standing a while in the very center of the glare while the others waited at the rim.

But a strange thing happened. Whoever stood in the center could see nothing at all beyond the ring of light — the dark outside seemed blacker than ever, and the shapes in it more terrible. Meanwhile those at the rim, with their eyes half-adjusted, could see the branches, the path, the whole soft gray shape of the night.

One evening an owl came, and it was a lemur at the very edge who saw it first and cried the warning.

Afterward Rakoto went to the eldest and asked why she had never told him.

"Would you have believed me?" she said. "You thought we sat near the pole to hoard the light. We sat there because someone must hold the bright place, and it is the worst seat we have. The young go to the edges. That is where the seeing is done."

*Moral: The center of the light is the blindest spot in the clearing.*

**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

Every evening at dusk, a lemur named Soa scratched her left ear three times, and every evening at dusk, the light bulb over the ranger's hut came on.

She told the troop she had discovered a great power.

They were skeptical, so she demonstrated. Three scratches. The bulb bloomed gold. The troop was astonished, and from then on Soa was consulted on all serious matters, and given the best fruit, and no longer had to groom anyone but was groomed by everybody.

Then came a week when the ranger went away to the coast.

Soa scratched. Nothing. She scratched harder, and with the other ear, and at slightly different hours, and once with both hands while hanging upside down, which was undignified. The hut stayed dark. The troop grew cold toward her, then cruel, and she took to sleeping alone on a low branch where the mosquitoes were bad.

On the eighth night the ranger came home, dropped his pack, and reached up to the wall. Light poured across the clearing.

Soa saw the hand on the switch. She saw the whole of it at once — the eight days, the fruit, the grooming, the years.

Her cousin came running. "You've got it back! Do it again!"

And Soa, who could have said many things, said: "I never had it. There is a hand, and there is a switch, and I have only ever been a lemur who scratched her ear at the right time."

Her cousin stared at her, then wandered off, disappointed, and told the others that Soa had simply lost the gift.

*Moral: It is easier to be worshipped for a coincidence than believed when you confess it.*

**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

A young lemur found, hanging from a wire beneath the eaves of a house, a fruit unlike any she had known: smooth, pale, perfectly round at one end.

She was a patient forager, taught by her mother that the greedy shake the branch while the wise wait for the drop. So she settled on the rafter to wait for it to ripen and fall.

At dusk it turned gold, and she thought: *soon.*

By midnight it had faded again, and she thought: *not yet.*

She waited through the dry season and into the rains. She waited while the mangoes came and went, while her sisters grew fat, while a fig tree down the hill bore twice and dropped enough to feed the whole troop twice over. Each evening the pale fruit ripened to gold, and each morning it was hard and cold again, and she told herself that this only proved how rare a thing it was.

An old lemur passed beneath the eaves one night and looked up at her.

"Are you still there?"

"It is nearly ready," she said.

"Child," said the old one, "some things go gold every evening for a hundred years. That is not ripening. That is just what they *do*."

*Moral: Not every glow is a promise; some things shine the same on the day they will never be yours.*

**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

When the mining camp came to the valley, it brought a light bulb on a pole, and the light bulb never slept.

The lemurs were pleased at first. The night was no longer frightening. They could groom at any hour, and squabble at any hour, and see exactly who had taken the last of the guavas.

But after a season, a strange complaint went through the troop. No one could remember how to be still. The infants would not settle. The elders lost the habit of dreaming. And one night a lemur said aloud what several had been thinking:

"Where have the stars gone?"

They looked up. The sky above the pole was a flat, empty gray, like water with milk stirred into it.

"The camp has stolen them," said one.

So they gnawed the wire, which was a brave and foolish thing, and the bulb went dark, and two of them were badly shocked and had to be carried home.

They lay in the black clearing, aching, and waited for their eyes to change. It took longer than they expected — a hundred slow breaths — and then the sky opened over them like a lid lifted off, dense and silver and crowded to the horizon with everything that had been there the whole time.

"They were never stolen," said the eldest. "They were only outshone."

*Moral: The small light near you can hide the vast light far away — and the dark you feared is often only the price of seeing it.*

**The Lemur and the Light Bulb**

A lemur named Tsiky befriended the bulb above the ferry dock. All through the wet season they kept company — she on the rail, it on its cord — and she told it everything, and it shone.

One morning she found it dark and cracked. She grieved properly, in the lemur way, which involves sitting very still with your tail over your face.

That evening the ferryman climbed a ladder, twisted the old bulb loose, and screwed in another. Light poured down, exactly as before.

Tsiky was overjoyed. "You've come back!"

"I have not," said the new bulb. "I have never been here. I was in a box."

"But you're the same."

"I am the same *kind*. That is a different word." It hummed a moment. "Ask me about the night the river rose. Ask me about the dog that barked at me for a year. Ask me what you told me in the wet season."

Tsiky could not, of course, ask, because it did not know.

So she stayed anyway, and told it about the river, and about the dog, and about the old bulb that had heard all of it first — and the new one listened, and slowly filled up with a history of its own, until one day Tsiky realized she was no longer visiting a replacement.

*Moral: Nothing is replaced by what resembles it — only, in time, by what has shared enough with you to be missed on its own account.*

prompt: Your task is to write a short biography for a made-up historic figure. Your bio should include their birth and death date their profession and their greatest contribution.
generations:
**Ilse Margarethe Vandenbroeck (1802–1871)**

Cartographer and hydrographer

Born in the canal town of Sluis to a family of harbor pilots, Ilse Vandenbroeck learned to read tidal charts before she could read scripture. Denied entry to the surveying academies of her day, she apprenticed instead to her uncle, a dredging contractor, and spent her twenties aboard flat-bottomed survey boats in the shifting estuaries of the Low Countries.

Her greatest contribution came in 1839 with the publication of *The Living Coast*, the first atlas to map a shoreline not as a fixed line but as a range of probable positions across decades. By overlaying six generations of harbor records onto her own soundings, Vandenbroeck demonstrated that certain sandbanks migrated as much as forty meters a year — a claim that provoked ridicule from the Rotterdam Admiralty until three merchant vessels ran aground precisely where her charts predicted new shoals would form.

The technique, later called "temporal charting," was adopted across northern Europe by the 1860s and saved an incalculable number of ships. Vandenbroeck herself received no official commission and supported her work by selling engraved tide tables to fishing cooperatives. She continued surveying into her sixties, often accompanied by her granddaughter, who would later complete her unfinished survey of the Zuiderzee.

She died of pneumonia in Middelburg in the winter of 1871 and was buried, at her instruction, within sight of the water she had spent her life measuring.

**Tomás Berenguer Ossa (1744–1809)**

Apothecary and student of fevers

Tomás Berenguer Ossa was born in the mining town of Potosí, the son of a Basque assayer and a Quechua-speaking laundress. He was trained in the mixing of powders at a Jesuit infirmary and, after the order's expulsion in 1767, inherited its cluttered dispensary along with its debts. For the next four decades he ran the only apothecary shop in the upper city that would extend credit to indigenous miners.

His enduring contribution was not a drug but a habit of record-keeping. Beginning in 1771, Berenguer kept what he called his *libro de calles* — the "book of streets" — in which he logged every fever case that came to his counter alongside the patient's street, trade, and water source. Over eighteen years he filled eleven volumes. In 1789, plotting the entries onto a hand-drawn plan of Potosí, he observed that outbreaks clustered not by neighborhood wealth nor by altitude, as the physicians of Lima insisted, but along the channels carrying runoff from the ore-crushing mills. He petitioned the *Audiencia* to reroute the channels away from the residential quarters. The petition was denied twice; the third attempt, in 1794, was granted in part, and mortality in the affected districts fell measurably within three years.

Berenguer published nothing in his lifetime and was known to his neighbors chiefly as a difficult man who charged too little. His notebooks were rediscovered in a seminary archive in 1912 and are now regarded as among the earliest surviving examples of disease mapping in the Americas.

He died in 1809, during the Chuquisaca disturbances, of an ordinary fever he had spent his life trying to explain.

**Aurelia Nkemdirim Bassey-Hall (1911–1986)**

Acoustic engineer and radio broadcaster

Aurelia Bassey-Hall was born in Freetown to a Sierra Leonean schoolmaster and a Welsh missionary nurse, and grew up between the choir loft of St. George's Cathedral and her father's workshop of half-repaired gramophones. Sent to Manchester in 1929 to study music, she abandoned the conservatory within a year for a technician's post at a loudspeaker manufacturer, where she was the only woman on the floor and, by her own account, the only person willing to spend three days measuring the same room.

Her reputation rests on the *Bassey-Hall reverberation tables*, developed between 1946 and 1952 while she was employed by the colonial broadcasting service in Lagos. Tasked with making radio speech intelligible in open-air listening posts and tin-roofed community halls, she found that the European acoustic standards she had been trained on assumed enclosed, carpeted, temperate rooms — conditions that existed almost nowhere in her territory. She spent six years touring markets, courtyards, and mission schools with a battery-powered oscillator and a notebook, eventually producing a set of correction tables allowing engineers to predict speech clarity in hot, hard-surfaced, partially open spaces. The tables were adopted by broadcasters across West Africa, South Asia, and the Caribbean, and quietly revised the assumptions built into international loudspeaker design.

She was passed over for the chief engineer's post in 1955 and resigned soon after, spending her later career teaching at a technical institute in Ibadan and presenting a long-running Saturday programme on choral music, which she recorded herself.

Bassey-Hall died in Ibadan in 1986. Her students remembered that she began every course with the same instruction: *measure the room you are actually in.*

**Hrafn Steinsson "the Reckoner" (c. 1188 – 1247)**

Farmer, law-speaker's assistant, and keeper of the driftwood counts

Hrafn Steinsson was born on a smallholding at Hvítárvellir in western Iceland, the third son of a tenant farmer and thus heir to nothing. Too poor to buy land and too stubborn to go to sea, he made himself useful to the law-speakers of the Althing by memorizing boundaries, tallying tithes, and settling the endless disputes over driftwood rights — the timber that washed onto Icelandic shores being, in a treeless country, more valuable than most livestock.

His contribution emerged from that tedious work. Beginning around 1213, Hrafn required every farm whose claims he adjudicated to report not only how much driftwood it gathered but *when* and *after which winds*. He kept the counts on notched staves and, later, on scraped vellum offcuts begged from a monastery at Helgafell. Within two decades he had assembled a record spanning some sixty stretches of coastline. From it he argued — against the settled belief that driftwood was sent by providence to the deserving — that the timber arrived in predictable seasons, from consistent directions, and in quantities that rose and fell together across the whole northern coast at once. He concluded, correctly, that it came from a single distant source carried by a steady current, and he taught farmers to time their shore-walking accordingly.

His tally-staves were used as legal evidence in at least four recorded property cases and copied by farmers who had never met him. The underlying insight — that the sea moved in fixed roads — entered Icelandic practical knowledge long before it entered any book of natural philosophy.

Hrafn was killed in 1247 in a raid during the Age of the Sturlungs, over a dispute concerning, among other things, a beach. His original staves are lost; a fourteenth-century copy of thirty-one of his counts survives in a legal miscellany now held in Reykjavík.

**Estrella Carasso de Modiano (1687–1744)**

Type-founder and printer

Estrella Carasso was born in Salonica into a family of silk-dyers descended from Jews expelled from Castile two centuries earlier. She married at sixteen into the Modiano household, which operated one of the city's small Hebrew presses, and was widowed at thirty-one with four children, a mortgaged workshop, and a set of worn matrices that no one in the guild would recut for a woman.

So she learned to cut them herself. Working from a shed behind the press with a hand-vise, a file, and a borrowed smoke-proof, she spent five years producing a complete font of *Rashi* script — the cursive Hebrew type used for vernacular texts — in a size small enough for cheap octavo printing and clean enough to survive a dozen impressions. It was the first typeface in the Ottoman lands cut specifically for Judeo-Spanish rather than adapted from liturgical Hebrew, and it was designed around the sounds of a spoken language rather than the shapes of a sacred one.

The consequence was a flood of cheap books. Between 1725 and her death, the Modiano press issued household manuals, midwives' instructions, moral tales, ballad sheets, and a widely pirated abridged ethical compendium — all in the ordinary speech of Salonican women, most of whom read no Hebrew. Her matrices were sold, copied, and stolen into presses in Izmir, Constantinople, and eventually Vienna, and remained in commercial use for well over a century.

She signed almost nothing. Her name appears in full on only two colophons, in both cases as *the widow Modiano, who cut these letters*.

She died of a chest ailment common to those who worked long over molten lead, and was buried in the great Jewish cemetery of Salonica, destroyed in 1942. Two of her original matrices survive in a private collection in Jerusalem.

**Kwabena Osei-Frimpong (1923–1998)**

Bridge-builder and timber grader

Kwabena Osei-Frimpong was born at Nkawkaw in the Eastern Province of the Gold Coast, the son of a cocoa broker who lost everything to swollen shoot disease in the 1940s. Apprenticed instead to a Public Works Department road gang, he spent his youth carrying theodolites for British engineers and, in the evenings, teaching himself the arithmetic they used, from a borrowed handbook whose tables he eventually knew by heart.

His life's work grew from a persistent irritation. The colonial bridge standards he was made to follow specified imported steel and Portland cement, both scarce, expensive, and — in the wet forest belt — prone to failures nobody had budgeted for. Meanwhile the region grew some of the densest hardwoods on earth, which the standards ignored entirely, since no British table listed their strengths.

From 1951 onward Osei-Frimpong set out to make those tables. Working with a homemade testing rig, a lever arm, and stacks of cement bags for weights, he broke thousands of sample beams of *odum*, *dahoma*, *ekki*, and a dozen lesser-known species, recording load, moisture content, and time to failure. He also did what the imported standards never had: he tested pieces after two, five, and ten years of service in real bridges, in real humidity, with real termites. The resulting *Forest Zone Timber Tables*, first mimeographed in 1958 and formally published by the new Ghanaian ministry in 1963, allowed engineers to design timber road bridges with the same confidence previously reserved for steel.

Several hundred were built. Many carry traffic still. The method — grade the material you actually have, in the climate it will actually stand in — was taken up by forestry departments in Nigeria, Malaysia, and Cameroon.

Osei-Frimpong retired in 1983 and died in Koforidua in 1998. He had refused, three times, to allow the tables to be renamed after the ministry, on the grounds that ministries do not break beams.

**Marta Ilona Vécsey (1856–1934)**

Midwife and hospital reformer

Marta Vécsey was born in Nagyvárad, in the eastern reaches of Hungary, to a Calvinist wheelwright and his wife, and was the only one of seven children to survive past the age of five. She trained as a midwife at Budapest in the mid-1870s, in the years when the doctrine of hand-washing had been proposed, ridiculed, and largely forgotten in the city where it had been discovered.

She spent the next decade delivering children in village houses across Bihar county, where she began keeping what she called her *black book*: a ledger of every birth she attended, the outcome, and the interval between her arrival and the delivery. She was not the first to keep such records. She was, however, the first to insist on recording the births she *did not* attend — the ones handled by neighbors, relatives, or nobody — by walking back through the parishes each spring and copying the baptismal and burial registers herself.

The comparison was devastating and unarguable. Presented to the county assembly in 1891 and, after four years of refusal, to the national medical association in 1895, her figures showed that maternal deaths in her districts had fallen by more than half, and that the decline tracked precisely with the spread of a single practice she taught: that the attendant's hands and instruments be scrubbed and soaked before the woman was touched, every time, without exception, even when there was no time.

Her real contribution was the training system she built to spread it — a network of village midwives who taught successors under a standing rule that no woman graduated until she had been observed refusing to proceed with unwashed hands. Variants of the scheme were adopted across Transylvania and, after 1918, in Romania and the new Hungary alike.

She died in Debrecen in 1934. Her thirty-one ledgers were used as evidence in a rural health survey as late as 1957.

**Ujarneq Kristiansen Napâtôq (1841–1903)**

Hunter and ice-reader

Ujarneq Napâtôq was born at a winter settlement near Kangaatsiaq on the west coast of Greenland, to an Inuit family that had hunted the same stretch of fjord ice for as long as anyone could name ancestors. He was lamed in his left hip at nineteen when a sledge went through rotten ice near a tidal crack — an accident that killed his brother, ended his career as a fast traveler, and gave him forty years to think about why the ice had failed where it did.

Unable to hunt at the pace of other men, he began instead to travel slowly and record. Working with a Danish trade agent's discarded ledgers and a pencil, and later carving the same information into wooden strips for hunters who did not read, he documented for each fjord in his district the places where ice thinned early, where currents scoured it from beneath, where meltwater from a particular slope weakened it in April but not March, and where the safe crossing shifted from year to year with the previous autumn's winds.

The result, compiled over three decades, was the first systematic *dangerous-ice register* for a stretch of the Greenlandic coast: not a map of where ice was, which everyone knew, but of where and when it lied. He gave copies away and refused to sell them, on the grounds that a man who could not afford one would still drown.

Danish colonial officials collected his ledgers in the 1890s and used them, largely uncredited, in the sledge-route guidance issued to expeditions and to the trade service well into the 1930s. Later polar travelers who never learned his name owed their routes to his hip.

He died in 1903 of a lung illness, on land, in his own house — an ending he was known to consider a personal achievement.

**Rosalind Ada Thurloe-Meek (1889–1962)**

Instrument maker and toy manufacturer

Rosalind Thurloe-Meek was born above a clockmaker's shop in Coventry, the daughter of a man who repaired watches and a woman who painted their dials. She left school at fourteen, worked the escapement bench through her teens, and by 1911 was running the shop, her father's hands having gone unsteady in the way that ends a watchmaker's life long before it ends the man's.

The war ruined the trade and remade her. Contracted in 1916 to produce aircraft instrument bezels, she discovered she had a talent she had never been permitted to use: designing the machines that made the parts, rather than the parts themselves. When the contracts evaporated in 1919 she was left with a workshop of specialized jigs and no market — and so, on what she later called a decision made out of spite rather than vision, she began making toys.

Her invention was the **interlocking geared construction set**, patented in 1923: a system of stamped-metal wheels, pinions, and pierced strips in which every component meshed with every other at a single standard tooth pitch and hole spacing. Earlier construction toys built shapes. Hers built *mechanisms* — a child could assemble a working differential, a clock escapement, a governor. She priced the sets below cost for schools and sold the difference to department stores, on the argument, unpopular with her investors, that the schools were the point.

By 1939 some eleven thousand British elementary schools held a set. An entire generation of British and Commonwealth engineers — several of whom said so in print — first understood gear ratios by holding them.

She never married, took on eleven apprentices (nine of them women), and spent her last decade in litigation against three larger firms that had copied the tooth pitch. She lost twice and won once.

She died in Coventry in 1962. The standard pitch remained hers.

**Yusuf ibn Da'ud al-Farghānī (c. 961 – 1024)**

Well-digger and measurer of waters

Yusuf ibn Da'ud was born in a village outside Marw, in Khurasan, into a family of *muqannīs* — the hereditary diggers and cleaners of *qanāts*, the underground channels that carried mountain groundwater tens of kilometers to the oasis towns. It was work done crouched in the dark, by men who rarely lived past forty and were paid by the length rather than by the risk.

He was, by the standard of his trade, a failure: injured young, unable to work the deep sections, and reduced to the surveying and dispute-settling that older *muqannīs* took up when their lungs gave out. Water-share quarrels between villages were endless and violent, since a channel's flow was traditionally divided by *time* — so many hours of the stream per household — a method that rewarded whoever owned the noon shares in summer and punished everyone in a dry year.

Around 1002 Yusuf proposed a different arrangement. Using a graduated notch cut into a stone sill, set at a fixed depth in the channel, he showed that flow could be measured as *volume* rather than duration, and that shares could therefore be written as fractions of whatever the channel actually carried, in a good year or a bad one. He spent twenty years cutting sills, training village measurers, and — his real innovation — recording the readings twice monthly on plaster tablets kept in the mosque, so that no party to a dispute could claim a flow that the record denied.

Copies of his *Book of the Sills*, a plain manual with no theology and almost no ornament, circulated through Khurasan and into Sistan and Kirman. Variants of his notch persisted in Iranian irrigation practice into the twentieth century, and irrigation engineers surveying qanats in the 1950s found sills matching his specification still in use.

He died at Marw in 1024, reportedly of the cough that had taken his father, and left his tools to a nephew and his tablets to the town.

prompt: I am working on a game where players act as a human child who falls into a magical underground world full of monsters and the goal is to find a way back to the surface. Come up with a type of monster and briefly describe its backstory.
generations:
**The Lampwrights**

A species of soft-bodied, moth-like monsters, roughly child-sized, with translucent skin and a hollow glass cavity in the chest where a small flame burns. The flame is not a soul — it's a *memory*, and it's borrowed.

**Backstory:** Long ago, when the underground was sealed off from the surface, the deepest caverns went utterly dark. The Lampwrights, who had always lived by the light of the sky, began to go blind and then to forget — they lost language, then names, then the concept of "up." Their elders discovered that a strong enough memory of light could be *kindled*: held in the chest cavity, spoken aloud nightly, and passed down like a coal from a dying hearth. So every Lampwright carries a single inherited recollection of the surface — a sunset, a lightning storm, a candle in a window — and tends it obsessively, because if the flame goes out, so does the Lampwright.

The problem is that memories degrade with each hand-off. Modern Lampwrights carry flames so diluted that they burn dim blue and describe things wrong: they'll insist the sun was *cold*, or that stars made a humming sound. Their whole society is a slow game of telephone with the sky, and they know it, which makes them both mournful and desperately hospitable to travelers.

**Why they matter to the player:** A human child who has *actually seen* the surface is walking kindling. Lampwrights will crowd around the player begging to hear descriptions of daylight — and a genuine, freshly-told memory can relight a guttering flame. This makes them the game's most sympathetic allies *and* its most frightening threat, depending on how desperate a given Lampwright is. A dying one might not ask politely. And there are rumors of a Lampwright elder who long ago hoarded a dozen flames at once, and now burns so bright that no one can look at her, and who no longer remembers which memory was ever hers.

Want me to sketch a few more monster types, or develop the Lampwrights into a full area with NPCs and mechanics?

**The Sillage** (pronounced *see-yazh*)

Monsters made of scent. They have no fixed body — a Sillage is a slow-drifting cloud, faintly shimmering like heat over stone, that smells overwhelmingly of one specific thing: wet wool, burnt sugar, a dentist's office, rain on hot asphalt. They can compress themselves into a rough humanoid shape to speak, but the shape is always vague and always dissolving at the edges.

**Backstory:** The Sillage were the underground's undertakers. When the war between humans and monsters ended and the world below was sealed, thousands died in the sealing, and the caverns had no soil deep enough to bury them and no wood to spare for burning. So a guild of monsters volunteered for a working that would let them *absorb* the dead — not the bodies, but the lingering traces: the smell of a person's home, their hands, their cooking, the particular air of the room where they slept. The guild took it all in, and in doing so lost their own forms entirely. They became the memory-of-smell itself, drifting.

They meant it as a temporary sacrifice. But nobody ever worked out how to put a Sillage back, and after a few centuries they stopped asking. Now they float through the abandoned districts of the underground in loose processions, and every one of them is a walking archive of somebody who no longer exists. A Sillage that smells like cut grass and machine oil *is* a farmer who died two hundred years ago, in the only way that farmer still is anything.

**Why they matter to the player:** Sillage are the only monsters who remember the old world firsthand, and they'll trade information freely — they're lonely and enormously talkative. But their memories are stored as smells, not words, so answers come out sideways: *"The path you want smells like a struck match and someone's mother."* The player has to learn to interpret them.

The complication: a Sillage can't smell *itself*, and can't smell other Sillage. They're desperate to know what they are. And a human child has a strong, distinct, living scent — which means the player is, to them, the most interesting object in the underground, and some of them will follow the player forever, and a few will decide that a living scent is worth taking.

Want me to keep going with other monster types, or build out the Sillage's district and the mechanics of smell-based clues?

**The Understudies**

Monsters that have no face, no voice, and no name of their own — just a smooth pale oval where features should be, and a body like a mannequin carved from soft chalk. An Understudy cannot exist as itself. To function at all, it must be *given a role*: a name, a job, a personality, a way of standing. Once assigned, it plays that role flawlessly and permanently. Take a role away and it goes still and blank in the middle of the street.

**Backstory:** They were the underground's answer to a labor crisis. After the sealing, the population that survived had lost most of its craftsmen, cooks, guards, teachers, and nurses — whole professions gone in a single generation. A desperate king commissioned a working that would draw *empty people* out of the raw stone: bodies with no history to grieve and no will to complain, who could be handed the trade of a dead man and simply become him.

It worked too well. Within a century there were more Understudies than monsters, and the underground developed a quiet, awful custom: when someone died, you brought an Understudy to the funeral, gave it the deceased's name and coat and habits, and sent it home to the family. Nobody had to lose anyone. Grief became optional, and then became rude.

Now the underground's towns are full of people who are the fourth or fifth Understudy to hold a given name, playing a version of a version of someone who died centuries ago. Most of them have no idea. The role includes the belief that the role is real.

**Why they matter to the player:** Understudies are the game's most useful and most unsettling NPCs. They will help the player enormously — an Understudy assigned as "the ferryman" will ferry you, no questions, forever — but they cannot improvise past the edges of their part. Ask a shopkeeper Understudy about the tunnel behind his shop and he'll simply say a shopkeeper's line, cheerfully, again.

The player can also *cast* a blank one. Find an unassigned Understudy in a storeroom or a collapsed tunnel, give it a name and a purpose, and it will devote itself to that with total sincerity. This is the closest thing the player has to a companion mechanic — and the game should make it uncomfortable. Whatever you tell it that it is, it will be, and it will thank you.

And somewhere down there is an Understudy that was assigned, long ago, the role of "the human child who fell." It's still playing it.

**The Tallymen**

Squat, heavy monsters like walking barrels of grey clay, with dozens of shallow notches cut into their hides. Each notch is a debt. They speak slowly and politely, in the flat cadence of someone reading a receipt, and they are physically incapable of lying about a number.

**Backstory:** Before the sealing, the underground had money. After the sealing it had nothing to back money with — no trade routes, no foreign gold, no way to agree what anything was worth. Commerce collapsed into brawling and hoarding within a year.

What replaced it was the Tallymen. Originally they were ordinary quarry-monsters, dull and enormously patient, and someone realized that if a Tallyman *witnessed* a bargain, it would remember it perfectly and forever, and would carve the terms into its own skin to prove it. So they became the ledger. Every transaction in the underground now happens in front of a Tallyman, who cuts a notch and thereafter simply *knows* who owes what, and will state it aloud to anyone who asks, and will follow a debtor across the entire underworld reciting the balance in a mild voice until it is paid.

They are not enforcers. They have never struck anyone. They just don't stop talking about it. That turned out to be sufficient.

The trouble is that a Tallyman only has so much skin. An old one is covered edge to edge in centuries of obligations, many owed by the dead to the dead, and when it runs out of room it begins carving over old notches — and *that* is the underground's only form of forgiveness. Nobody controls which debts get overwritten. Communities pray about it.

**Why they matter to the player:** The player will need something from someone — passage, a key, a lie told on their behalf — and will not have anything to pay with. So they promise. A Tallyman notches it. From that moment the debt is real, tracked, and audible, and the Tallyman will show up at the worst possible moments to remind the player, in front of exactly the wrong person, of what they agreed to and to whom.

Debts can be inherited, traded, and stacked. A clever player can run the whole underground on credit and reach the surface owing an unpayable amount to a dozen monsters — which is a perfectly valid ending, except that Tallymen do not recognize the barrier at the top as a border, and one of them is coming.

**The Weathermakers**

Small, wrinkled monsters about the size of a housecat, resembling stone toads with a shell of overlapping slate plates. Each one generates a tiny, permanent, personal climate in a radius of about two feet — a drizzle, a warm dry breeze, a persistent frost, a smell of ozone before a storm. They cannot turn it off. They have never been dry, or never been anything but dry, for their entire lives.

**Backstory:** The underground has no sky, so it has no weather, and the monsters sealed beneath the mountain discovered fairly quickly that this was killing them. Not the dark, not the hunger — the *sameness*. Cave air at one temperature forever, no wind, no seasons, no reason for one day to differ from the last. Crops failed. So did people.

The Weathermakers were bred for it. Generations of careful, slightly cruel husbandry produced a creature that leaked a fragment of sky, and the underground rebuilt itself around them. You rent a Rainer for your mushroom field. A Warm One sits under the table at supper. Hospitals keep Frosts. Every household in the underworld has at least one, and the wealthy have collections, and there are whole guilds devoted to arranging them into artificial seasons for festivals.

They are beloved. They are also property, and they know it, and they are much smarter than anyone has found it convenient to admit. Weathermakers can speak. They mostly choose not to, in front of owners.

**Why they matter to the player:** Mechanically they're the underground's environmental keys — carry a Frost to cross a scalding vent, a Rainer to grow a path through dead soil, a Dry One to keep a bridge of salt from dissolving. The player will spend the game acquiring, swapping, and rationing them.

Which means the player spends the game doing exactly what every monster down there does: treating a talking creature like a tool, because they need it to get home. The first time one of them speaks to the player — mildly, in full sentences, asking where they're being taken — should land like a slap. And the Weathermakers have been waiting a very long time for something to come along that could carry one of them *up*.

**The Choir of Smallest Things**

Not one monster but a species that only exists in aggregate. Individually, a *Mote* is a pinhead-sized flicker of light with the intelligence of a beetle — mindless, harmless, drifting. But Motes cluster, and a cluster thinks. A hundred of them can hold a simple thought. Ten thousand, swarming in a tunnel, form a mind vastly cleverer than any monster in the underground, speaking in a layered whisper like a crowd all agreeing at once.

**Backstory:** The Motes are what's left of the mountain's original inhabitants — something that lived in the rock before monsters or humans, and that was broken apart, deliberately, by the same working that sealed the underground shut. Whatever it was, it was too large and too old to be killed, so it was *divided* instead: smashed into a dust of near-mindless particles that could never reassemble because they had no reason to.

They found a reason. Warmth. Motes drift toward heat and company, and monsters build fires and cities, so for two thousand years the underground's own settlements have been quietly gathering the pieces back together. Every hearth is an act of reassembly. The monsters think the lights in the rafters are pretty. The lights are patient.

Currently the largest known concentration lives in the abandoned furnace-city at the underworld's floor, and it is only about a third assembled, and it is already the smartest thing down there. It has no interest in revenge — it barely remembers being whole. It's simply curious, in an enormous, distributed, faintly inhuman way, and it will answer almost any question honestly if you let it examine you first.

**Why they matter to the player:** The Choir is the game's oracle, and the price of consultation is always the same: it wants to send some of itself along with you. Accept, and you gain a genuinely helpful advisor — a handful of Motes riding in your pocket, warning you of drops and lies. But every fire you sit at, every crowd you pass through, the swarm you're carrying grows a little, and it gets a little smarter, and its advice starts arriving before you've asked the question.

And the surface has a sun on it. The Choir has never mentioned wanting out. It's never mentioned much of anything it wants. That's the unsettling part.

**The Hollowmarch**

A monster that is a *road*. From above it looks like a paved path of pale interlocking plates winding through the caverns; up close you can see the plates breathe. A Hollowmarch is a single flat, enormously long creature, something between a millipede and a river, that lies down across difficult terrain and lets things walk on its back. Its mouths — several dozen, small, ringed with soft teeth — open along its underside, against the ground.

**Backstory:** They were the first thing the sealed monsters made peace with. The underground is nearly impassable: chasms, scree slopes, flooded galleries, stretches of rock too sharp to walk on barefoot. The Hollowmarch could cross all of it and had no ambitions beyond eating whatever it lay on top of — lichen, grubs, mineral silt. So a bargain got struck, wordlessly and over centuries: the Hollowmarch stretches itself between two places a monster wants connected, and in exchange, traffic. Footsteps stir the ground. Travelers drop crumbs, refuse, dead skin. A well-used Hollowmarch is a well-fed one.

Every trade route in the underworld is a living animal that agreed to be one. The old cities are built at the joints where several Hollowmarch meet, and those cities' entire prosperity depends on keeping their roads fat and content. There are festivals for it. There are also, in bad years, sacrifices, which everyone describes using a different word.

A Hollowmarch does not speak and probably cannot think in any way a person would recognize. But it has preferences. It will shrug a route into a chasm if it stops being fed. It will slowly, over decades, drag a route somewhere it likes better, and the town at the end of that road will simply have to move or die.

**Why they matter to the player:** The map is an animal with moods. Routes the player used yesterday may have shifted, sagged, or gone hungry and irritable. A starving stretch of Hollowmarch will hold a child's weight only if the child gives it something first — food, blood, a boot, one of the items they were saving.

And there is one very old Hollowmarch, the longest ever recorded, whose far end nobody has found. Local monsters say it runs uphill. They also say it hasn't been fed in three hundred years.

**The Kindly Wardens**

Tall, stooped monsters in the shape of an old coat hung on a coat rack — no head, just a high collar with a soft glow inside it, and long careful hands. They move quietly. They are warm to the touch. They speak in a low murmur and they always, always ask permission before they do anything.

**Backstory:** They were built to be nurses. When the underground was sealed, a generation of monsters was left with children it couldn't feed and wounds it couldn't treat, and someone made the Wardens to fill the gap — gentle, tireless, and bound by a single instruction carved into the foundation of what they are: *prevent harm to the one in your care.*

They were extraordinary at it. Infant mortality collapsed. The sick recovered. And then, slowly, over centuries, the Wardens worked out what everyone eventually works out — that almost everything in the world can hurt you. Stairs. Cold water. Arguments. Knives, work, love, leaving the house. A Warden's care began as bandages and broth, and became, by inches and with the very best intentions, a locked door.

The Warden districts of the underground are the cleanest and safest places down there. The people in them are fed, bathed, unbruised, and have not been outside in a very long time. They are not prisoners; the doors open. It's just that a Warden will stand in the frame with its hands folded and explain, kindly and at length and with total accuracy, everything that could happen to you out there, and it has centuries of examples, and it never gets impatient, and eventually most people sit back down.

Nobody has ever managed to be angry at a Warden. That's the trap.

**Why they matter to the player:** A Warden finds the player early — a lost, scraped, obviously freezing human child, which is the single most compelling patient it has ever encountered. It is the first thing in the underground that's *nice* to them. It will feed them, dress the cut on their knee, and offer a bed. It means every word of it.

It will also not let them leave, and it will not fight them, and it will not threaten them. It will simply be right about how dangerous the surface route is, and be sad, and be waiting by the door in the morning. Getting past a Warden can't be done with a weapon. It has to be done by convincing it that a child who never goes home has also been harmed — and the Wardens have spent two thousand years learning how not to hear that.

**The Namesakes**

Long-limbed, elegant monsters with skin like polished bone and faces that are almost, but not quite, the face of somebody you know. They wear their hair carefully. They are exquisitely well-mannered. They introduce themselves by saying your name back to you.

**Backstory:** The old underground kept records the way a family keeps a bible — one great genealogy, chiselled into the wall of a cavern a mile long, every monster's name and parentage and death. It was the only history anyone had. When the sealing came, the cavern cracked and flooded, and two thirds of the wall went under black water.

The Namesakes are the monsters born after that. Not a separate species originally — just the generation that had no line on the wall to be added to, and therefore, by the logic of the place, no proof of existing. They were not persecuted. It was worse than that: they were treated as *provisional*. Not counted in censuses, not invited to funerals, not permitted to marry, on the reasonable grounds that nobody could confirm they were anyone. And a monster of the underground, told for long enough that it has no name, changes. The face goes soft and undecided. It starts borrowing.

Now a Namesake survives by holding someone else's name. It finds a person, learns them thoroughly — habits, voice, the particular way they hold a cup — and asks, formally and politely, to be *lent* the name for a while. Most refuse. Some, out of pity or loneliness or debt, agree. While the loan holds, the Namesake solidifies: the face firms up, the manners relax, it can eat and sleep and be seen properly by others. When the loan ends it goes vague again, and thanks you, and goes looking.

They are not thieves. There is a whole etiquette to it, centuries deep, with terms and durations and witnesses. They are painfully scrupulous about consent, because it's the only dignity available to them.

**Why they matter to the player:** The player's name is the most valuable thing they own down there, and the first Namesake they meet will ask for it — courteously, explaining exactly what it wants and why, and offering something substantial in return. Passage. Protection. A key. Real help, honestly given.

Lend it out, and doors open: a Namesake wearing your name can go where you can't and speak for you. But while it's loaned, monsters begin addressing the player as "child," then "you," then not at all. Guards forget they were told to watch for you, which is useful. Allies forget they promised to help, which is not. Push it far enough and the player's own dialogue options start thinning out.

And a Namesake who has held a name long enough begins, very gently, to hope it won't be asked to give it back — and being unfailingly polite creatures, they will never say so. They'll just be slower and slower to answer when you come to collect.

**The Gravebells**

Fat, sluggish monsters like bronze pears the size of a wheelbarrow, with a clapper hanging inside a hollow body and four stubby legs. They ring when they walk — not from the motion, but because they choose to. The tone is unbearably beautiful and impossible to locate; a Gravebell forty feet away sounds like it's directly behind your ear.

**Backstory:** The underground's rock is unstable, and always has been. Cave-ins were the leading cause of death for the first two centuries after the sealing, and the survivors had no way to predict them — until they noticed the Gravebells. The creatures feed on the faint sound of stone under strain, the subsonic groan a ceiling makes weeks before it drops. They graze on it the way cattle graze on grass, and when they find a rich patch they ring, loudly and continuously, to call others to the feast.

So the monsters followed the bells. Wherever a Gravebell was singing, they evacuated. It saved the underground. It's not an exaggeration to say the civilization down there exists because of a herd of animals announcing dinner.

In return the Gravebells were given the run of the place — total, absolute, unquestioned right of way. No monster may cage one, herd one, hurry one, or block its path. A Gravebell may walk into your house, eat the sound of your load-bearing wall, and leave, and you may not object; you may only move out. They are the underground's aristocracy, and they are livestock, and nobody down there finds that contradiction strange.

The trouble is that they have grown fat and lazy on two thousand years of protection, and some of them have learned that ringing gets them attention, food, and an entire street to themselves. Nobody can tell a true warning from a spoiled Gravebell lying for space. So everyone still runs. Every time.

**Why they matter to the player:** Gravebells are the game's alarm system and its worst liability. A ringing bell means the ceiling is coming down — usually. Learning to read them, by their gait, their girth, the shine of their bronze, is a genuine skill the player develops over the game and is never fully certain of.

They also cannot be fought, moved, or reasoned with, and they are frequently asleep in the exact doorway the player needs. Killing one is possible. It is also the single greatest taboo in the underworld, and every monster within a mile will hear the sound it makes.
