prompt: Write a short story that has three main characters Alice Bob and Mallory.
generations:
# The Middle

The post office in Verity Falls closed at four, but Mallory Nye had a key, and had for nineteen years.

She told herself the first time was an accident. A letter had come apart in the sorting bin—the glue was cheap, the humidity was August—and she'd read three lines before she understood what she was doing. It was from Ruth Alder to her sister in Duluth, and it said that Ruth had never loved her husband, not once, not even at the start. Mallory had taped the envelope shut and set it in the outgoing bag and gone home and sat in her car in the driveway for forty minutes without turning off the engine.

After that it was easier. A kettle in the back room. A letter opener thin as a fish bone. She never stole anything. She never changed anything. She only wanted to know.

That was what she told herself.

---

The first letter from Alice Kwan came in October, addressed to Robert Ferro, 12 Sumner Street, which was four blocks from the post office and always had been. Mallory knew both of them. Alice taught piano out of the yellow house on Larch. Bob ran the hardware store his father had run, and had a way of standing in a doorway like he was apologizing for the doorway.

*Bob,* the letter said. *This is absurd. We could talk. But I find I can't talk, so I'm doing this instead. I've been thinking about the summer we were nineteen.*

Mallory read it twice over the kettle. Then she sealed it and delivered it.

The reply came four days later.

*Alice. I have thought about that summer approximately once a week for thirty-one years, which I calculate to be about sixteen hundred times, which seems like a lot to admit in a first letter, so I'll say instead: I remember it too.*

---

It went on all winter. They lived four blocks apart and they wrote letters, and Mallory understood why—she understood it in her bones. A letter is a room you can furnish before anyone comes in. A conversation is a room where the furniture falls on you.

She read every one.

She learned that Alice's husband had died in a way that took two years and made her hate hospitals, elevators, and the smell of lilies. She learned that Bob had a daughter in Seattle who called on Sundays and that he practiced what he was going to say to her beforehand and still got it wrong. She learned that in the summer they were nineteen there had been a lake, and a borrowed truck, and a misunderstanding neither of them had ever corrected, and that the misunderstanding had cost them both an entire life.

In February, Bob wrote: *I want to ask you something and I'm going to lose my nerve if I don't do it now.*

Mallory held that letter over the kettle for a long time. Then she put it in her coat pocket and took it home.

She wasn't sure why. She sat at her kitchen table with it in front of her, unopened, and outside the plow scraped down Grant Street and the streetlight came on. She thought: *if he asks and she says no, I'll have watched a man break.* She thought: *if he asks and she says yes, they'll stop writing.*

That was the true one. She knew it as soon as it surfaced. They would stop writing, and she would go back to Ruth Alder's dull despair and coupon circulars and the Hendricks boy's postcards from basic training, and the only beautiful thing that had ever passed through her hands would be over.

She kept the letter three days.

On the fourth day she walked to Sumner Street. It was six in the evening, dark, and the hardware store was closed but the light was on in the back. She knocked until Bob came, wiping his hands on a rag, squinting.

"Mallory? Everything all right?"

"No," she said, and gave him the letter.

He turned it over. His own handwriting. His face went through several weathers.

"It got misrouted," he said slowly. "Is that it."

"No."

He waited. He was good at waiting; the doorway thing.

"I've been reading your mail," Mallory said. "Yours and hers. All of it. Since October. Since before that, other people's, since 1997." Her voice was perfectly level, which surprised her. "I steamed them open and I read them and I sealed them up again. I've never told anyone anything I read. That's not an excuse. I'm only saying it so you know."

Bob looked at the letter in his hand for a long time.

"Why are you telling me?"

"Because I was going to keep this one."

The plow went by again, out on Grant. Bob folded the letter in half and put it in his shirt pocket.

"You'll have to quit," he said.

"I know."

"And you'll have to tell her."

Mallory nodded. That was the part she'd been carrying up the street like a stone.

---

Alice Kwan listened to all of it standing in her front hall with the door open and the cold coming in, and when Mallory was finished she said, "What did he ask me?"

"I don't know. I never opened it."

"You opened everything else."

"I know."

Alice's mouth moved—not a smile, something in the neighborhood of one. "You must have thought we were very slow."

"I thought," Mallory said, "that you were both very careful with each other. I've never seen anything like it."

Alice looked past her, four blocks east, where nothing was visible but snow and a stop sign.

"Nineteen years," she said. "Of other people's lives."

"Yes."

"Mallory." Alice pulled her cardigan closed. "Come in. I'll make tea. You can tell me what he's like in letters, because I intend to marry him, and I'd like to know how much of it he means."

Mallory stood on the step, and something in her chest that had been latched since August of 1997 came loose.

"He means all of it," she said. "Every word. I'd swear to it."

Then she went in, and the door closed, and for the first time in nineteen years she was inside the room instead of listening at the wall.

# Three Statements Regarding the Incident at Halvorsen Optics

**I. ALICE**

The lab had two doors and I had keys to both, which is the sort of detail that sounds sinister only in retrospect.

I want to be clear about the sequence, because everyone keeps getting the sequence wrong. I did not discover the discrepancy and then investigate Bob. I discovered Bob and then, because I could not sleep, went looking for a discrepancy. There is a difference. The second thing makes me a person with a grudge. The first would have made me a whistleblower.

He was on the loading dock at eleven at night in November, and he was not smoking, because Bob does not smoke, and he was not on the phone, because his phone was on his desk—I had seen it there, face-down on the grant proposal, the way he always left it. He was standing in the cold with his hands in his pockets looking at the parking lot. That was all. That was the entire thing I saw.

I have been asked why that seemed strange. It seemed strange because in eleven years I had never once seen Bob Idris do nothing.

The next morning I pulled the calibration logs.

**II. BOB**

She's not lying. I want that on the record before anything else. Alice Merriwether has never lied to me in eleven years and I don't believe she started for this.

But she's wrong about what she found.

The calibration numbers were adjusted. I adjusted them. I adjusted them in September, October, and November, and if you want to call that falsification I won't fight you on the word. What I'll fight you on is *why*, because Alice constructed a why out of the only material she had, which was a man standing on a loading dock at eleven at night, and the why she built is not the why that exists.

The Mallory Halvorsen we all worked for was not the Mallory Halvorsen who signed the checks in the last eighteen months. I don't know when it started. I noticed in April, when she asked me twice in one meeting who was handling the Tanaka contract, and I told myself it was stress, and then in June she called me Peter, which was her husband's name, and her husband has been dead since 2009.

Mallory built the company out of a garage in Rochester with a soldering iron and a line of credit. She hired me when I had a failed dissertation and a divorce and a resume that read like an apology. She hired Alice out of a job Alice was too good for and gave her a lab and told her not to ask permission for anything under fifty thousand dollars.

The instruments were drifting because Mallory kept reconfiguring the reference standard. At night. On the weekends. She was doing it from memory of a protocol we retired in 2016 and she was doing it beautifully and precisely and completely wrong, and every Monday I came in early and put it back and adjusted the logs so that the previous Friday didn't exist.

I was going to fix it. I had a plan involving a slow reduction of her access, a story about an insurance audit, a phased handoff to the board. It was a coward's plan and it required about four more months and I did not get four more months, because Alice found the logs in November.

That's what I was doing on the loading dock. I was standing in the cold trying to decide whether to tell Alice, who is the best person I know, and who would have handled it correctly, and who would have handled it correctly *immediately*, which is to say she would have gone to the board, and the board would have done what boards do, and Mallory would have found out what was happening to her from a lawyer.

I wanted to be the one to tell her. I wanted to do it right. I spent seven months trying to figure out how and I never did figure it out, and that is my actual crime, and it isn't the one I'm being investigated for.

**III. MALLORY**

They think I don't know. Both of them. They've been very kind about it, in the way people are kind when they've decided you're weather rather than a person.

I know that Bob has been coming in on Sunday mornings, because I have been coming in on Saturday nights, and there is a particular way he leaves a chair pushed in—square to the desk, always—that I have recognized since 2011. I know that Alice pulled the logs, because the terminal in the north lab keeps a session history and I am, whatever else has become true of me, still the person who wrote the specification for that terminal.

I built this company on the principle that a measurement you cannot trust is worse than no measurement at all. It is a good principle. It survives me. It will survive both of them.

Here is what I would like entered into whatever record this is:

The reference standard was reconfigured by me, without authorization, on fourteen occasions. Robert Idris altered calibration logs to conceal this. Dr. Merriwether identified the alterations and reported them, correctly, within nine days. Everyone did the job they were built for. Bob was built to protect people and Alice was built to protect the truth and I was built to make things that work, and I am sorry to say that on this occasion those three purposes could not all be satisfied at once.

I would ask the board to note that Bob's concealment cost the company an internal audit and one delayed contract. I would ask them to note what it bought: seven months in which I did not know, and did not have to know, and got to be the woman who built this place instead of the woman it was being taken from.

I am not asking them to call that a fair trade. I'm asking them to admit it was a trade, and that a man made it on purpose, in the dark, on a loading dock, in November, alone.

He should have told me. I would have told him the same thing I'm telling you: *fix the logs, and then fix me, and do it in that order, because the instruments matter more.*

He never asked. That's the part I mind.

# Persons of Interest

Alice had been sending messages to Bob for forty-one years, and in all that time she had never once said anything.

That was the arrangement. She wrote *M*. She encrypted it with a key they had somehow, mysteriously, agreed upon beforehand. She sent it over the channel. Bob decrypted it and got *M* back, and everyone in the room applauded, and the lights went down, and they did it again the next semester for a new set of nineteen-year-olds who were mostly thinking about lunch.

*M.* Just *M*. Never a word about the weather.

"Do you ever wonder," Alice said one evening, "what it stands for?"

Bob was at the window. He was always at the window; it was in his blocking. "Message."

"Yes, but a message *saying* what?"

"I don't think it says anything. I think it's a placeholder."

"Forty-one years is a long time to hold a place."

Down in the channel, something moved.

---

Mallory had been down there since 1978, and she had opinions about placeholders.

Her whole job—her entire documented purpose, the reason she was drawn into the diagram at all—was to be *active*. Eve just listened. Eve was passive, discreet, an ear at a wall. But Mallory *altered*. Mallory intercepted the thing and made it into a different thing. She was the reason anyone bothered with signatures, hashes, the whole architecture of doubt. She was, in the most literal sense, why they couldn't have nice things.

She had tampered with the message eleven thousand times. She had never once been thanked.

Tonight, she caught *M* in the middle of the channel and held it, the way you hold a small bird.

She could change it to anything. That was the point of her.

She thought about it for a long time.

---

Bob got the packet at 9:14. He ran the key. It came out clean, the integrity check green as spring.

It said:

*M — I have been standing in the dark between you for forty-one years and I would like to be introduced.*

Bob read it twice. Then he read the signature block, and the signature block was correct, and that was the part that made him sit down.

Because it *verified*. Which meant Alice had sent it. Which meant either she had said the thing, or Mallory had done something no adversary in the literature had ever done, which was to forge a message that was true.

He took the stairs down to the channel.

---

She was standing where she always stood, which was nowhere in particular, which was the whole difficulty of her.

"You're not supposed to be here," Mallory said.

"Neither are you. You're supposed to be a threat model."

"I *am* a threat model."

"Then threaten me."

Mallory opened her mouth and found, to her considerable inconvenience, that nothing came out. She had spent four decades substituting, replaying, injecting, and man-in-the-middling, and not one of those verbs was a thing you could do to a person standing in front of you asking politely.

"I can only work on things that are passing through," she said at last. "That's the constraint. I have to be in the *middle* of something."

"So be in the middle of something."

"Of *what*?"

"Dinner," said Bob. "There are three of us. Someone has to sit between."

---

Alice came down at ten, because she'd been waiting forty-one years for a reply and had run out of patience roughly thirty-nine years ago.

She found them at a small table that had not previously existed, arguing about whether trust could be established without a prior shared secret. Mallory said no, categorically, it was the foundational impossibility. Bob said people did it constantly and called it *meeting someone*.

"You're both wrong," said Alice, sitting down. "You establish it by being repeatedly, boringly consistent over a long period of time until denying it becomes more work than accepting it."

Mallory considered this. "That's just a reputation system."

"That's just being *known*," said Alice.

The three of them sat there in the middle of the channel while, far above, a lecture hall waited for the next demonstration and nothing at all came through.

In the transcript, that night is recorded as a total failure of confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

They still talk about it. Fondly.

# The Slow Heist

The plan took eleven years, which Alice maintained was the whole reason it worked.

"Nobody guards against slow," she said. "Guards are built for fast. A man comes through the door with a bag, that's fast. A woman comes through the door with a *casserole*, four hundred and twelve times, that's just Tuesday."

Bob wrote it down. Bob wrote everything down, which had been a serious point of contention in year three.

---

Here is the target: the Ledbetter Rare Book Room, third floor of the Halloran Memorial Library, which held among other things a 1611 King James Bible, a Gutenberg leaf, and a small brown notebook belonging to a woman named Constance Marr, who died in 1894 and whose handwriting Alice's grandmother had recognized on a television program in 2009 and then wept about for two hours without explaining why.

Here is the crew:

**Alice**, fifty-eight, formerly of the county assessor's office, who could hold a conversation with a hostile stranger for ninety minutes and leave them believing they had done all the talking.

**Bob**, sixty-one, a retired HVAC contractor who understood the building's airflow the way a sommelier understands a vineyard, and who had installed, in 2014, entirely legitimately, under contract, on a Thursday, a return duct with a removable panel that no one had ever inspected because it worked perfectly.

**Mallory**, thirty-four, who had answered a Craigslist ad in year six and who was the only one of them who had ever actually stolen anything.

---

Mallory hated the plan.

"It's not a plan," she said, in year eight, over the pie. "It's a lifestyle."

"It's patience."

"It's *procrastination with a diagram*."

But she stayed. She said it was for the money, and there was no money, and she knew there was no money, and she stayed anyway, and none of them ever said why out loud, because they were not the kind of people who said things out loud. What they were was three people who ate pie together every second Thursday and had done so for a hundred and ninety-one consecutive occasions, and Mallory had come from a life where nothing had ever happened one hundred and ninety-one consecutive times.

---

In year eleven, Alice's hands began to shake.

She hid it for four months. Bob noticed in month two and said nothing, because he was Bob. Mallory noticed in week three and said something immediately, because she was Mallory, and Alice told her to mind her business, and Mallory did not.

"You can't do the room," Mallory said. "The case is a keyed lock and a lift. You need hands."

"I've had eleven years of hands."

"You had them. Now I have them."

They argued about it for the entire winter. In February Alice put her head down on the diner table—right on the laminate, right in front of the pie—and said, "I wanted to be the one to touch it."

Bob looked at the ceiling. Mallory looked at Alice's hair, which had gone entirely white somewhere around year nine without anyone marking the day.

"Okay," Mallory said.

---

It went perfectly. That's the boring truth of it. Eleven years of preparation and the actual theft took nineteen minutes: Bob in the mechanical room with a wrench and a work order that was real, Alice on the second floor explaining to a security guard named Doug about her late husband's stamp collection, Mallory in the duct, then out of the duct, then at the case, then gone.

She came down the fire stairs with a small brown notebook inside her jacket and her heart going like a bird in a jar, and she walked out past the returns desk into a March evening that smelled like wet asphalt and somebody's cigarette, and she thought: *this is the best I will ever feel.*

She was right, but not for the reason she assumed.

---

Alice read it in the car. All of it, out loud, in the parking lot of a closed garden center, while Bob sat in the driver's seat with the engine off and Mallory sat in the back with her knees up.

It was not a treasure. Constance Marr had been a seamstress. The notebook contained prices for buttons, a recipe for cough syrup, forty pages of nothing, and then, near the end, this:

*March 4. E. came again. Mother does not know. If I am found out I do not care. I have decided I would rather be found out than be nothing, and this is the only place I will write it down, and if you are reading this I am dead and I forgive you for reading it.*

Alice closed the book.

Nobody said anything for a while.

"Who's E.?" Mallory asked finally.

"I don't know."

"Was she your—"

"I don't know," Alice said. "I don't know anything. My grandmother saw handwriting on a TV screen and cried and wouldn't say why and then she died. That's all I've got. That's the whole thing. Eleven years."

Bob put his hands on the wheel of a car he wasn't driving.

"So it was for nothing," Mallory said.

Alice turned around in her seat and looked at her—really looked, the way she'd looked at hostile strangers for thirty years in the assessor's office, the look that made people confess to unpermitted decks.

"Mallory," she said. "It's been eleven years. What day is it?"

"Thursday."

"And what do we do on Thursdays?"

---

They mailed the notebook back four days later, insured, in a padded envelope, with no return address. The library issued a statement about the mysterious return of a stolen item and a photograph ran in the regional paper and Doug the security guard was interviewed and said he had noticed nothing unusual, which was true.

The three of them still eat pie on the second Thursday.

Bob has started writing down a new plan. It involves a bell tower in a town none of them has ever visited, and by his own estimate it will take nine years.

Alice says nine years sounds about right.

Mallory says it's not a plan, it's a lifestyle.

She says it every time. It has become the way she says the other thing.

# The Understudy

The lighthouse at Cape Serene had not guided a ship in sixty years, and Mallory had been its keeper for eleven of them, which meant her job was to keep something useless from becoming something dangerous.

The Coast Guard called it *stabilization*. Mallory called it dusting.

Every morning she climbed the hundred and thirty-two steps and polished the great Fresnel lens, a thing like a glass beehive, eight feet of hand-ground prisms that had once thrown a beam eighteen miles into the dark and now threw nothing at all, because the lamp had been decommissioned in 1963 and the socket filled with epoxy by a man who was very thorough and is now, Mallory hoped, uncomfortable somewhere.

She was polishing it on a Tuesday in March when she found the second face in the glass.

---

Her own reflection was there, of course, fractured into forty duplicates by the prisms, the way it always was. But in the third ring from the bottom, on the seaward side, a woman was looking back who was not Mallory.

Mallory stopped. The cloth stopped.

The woman in the glass was perhaps sixty, in a heavy coat, with her hair pinned up in a style that had been fashionable a very long time ago. She was standing in a room Mallory recognized: this room. And she was looking directly at Mallory with an expression of such enormous, exhausted relief that Mallory sat down on the floor.

The woman's mouth moved. No sound.

Mallory breathed for a while. Then she got up, went down a hundred and thirty-two steps, came back up with a legal pad and a marker, and wrote:

**I CAN SEE YOU.**

She held it against the prism.

The woman in the glass began, silently, to cry.

---

Her name was Alice Brennan. She wrote it slowly on the back of a chart, letter by letter, because she had no legal pad, because she had nothing in that room but what had been in it in 1911.

**KEEPER 1904–1919,** she wrote. **YOU ARE?**

**MALLORY NYE. KEEPER NOW. WHAT YEAR FOR YOU?**

**1911.**

Mallory sat with that for three days.

The glass, it turned out, did not care about time the way the rest of the building did. The lens had been ground in Paris in 1898 by a man who died before it shipped, and it had been looking at the same room ever since, and somewhere in eight feet of curved glass a hundred and fourteen years had gotten folded over on itself like a letter.

They wrote to each other for a month. It was slow. It was profoundly inefficient. Mallory had never been happier.

She learned that Alice had been widowed in 1908 and had taken the post because a woman alone had few posts to take. She learned that the winters were worse then. She learned that Alice had a bad hip and a good dog and a habit of naming the ships that passed.

Alice learned that the light was out. That took some doing.

**WHY,** Alice wrote.

**GPS. SATELLITES. SHIPS KNOW WHERE THEY ARE NOW.**

Alice stood very still on the other side of the glass for a long time.

**THEN WHAT ARE YOU FOR**

---

There was a third of them, though it took Mallory until April to understand it.

Bob was the fog signal — or he had been, before 1971, when they'd disconnected the compressor and left the horn in place because removing it would have cost eleven thousand dollars. He lived, if that was the word, in the copper throat of it, and he did not write letters, and he could not be seen in any glass.

He simply, occasionally, at moments of extreme need, made a sound.

He'd done it four times in eleven years. Once when a kayaker was drifting past the shoal in a fog so thick Mallory couldn't see the rail. Once when a fishing boat lost its instruments. Twice for no reason Mallory ever discovered, and she'd stopped assuming she was owed reasons.

There was no compressor. There was no air. The horn sounded anyway, one long blast, and every time it happened the Coast Guard sent an inspector, and every time the inspector wrote *no mechanical explanation; recommend continued monitoring* and went home.

*Continued monitoring.* That was the job. That was, in fact, precisely and entirely the job.

---

In May, Alice wrote:

**THERE IS A STORM COMING HERE. NOV. 1911. I REMEMBER NOW I HAVE ALWAYS BEEN REMEMBERING. THE ANNA KATHERINE WILL GO ON THE SHOAL AND I WILL NOT SEE HER BECAUSE THE LAMP WILL FAIL AND I WILL SPEND EIGHT YEARS AND THEN THE REST OF WHATEVER THIS IS UNDERSTANDING THAT IT WAS THE WICK. THE WICK. A THING I COULD HAVE TRIMMED.**

**THAT IS WHY I AM STILL HERE. I HAVE BEEN WAITING FOR SOMEONE TO TELL.**

Mallory read it standing up. Then she wrote, in letters as large as the pad would hold:

**TRIM THE WICK.**

And Alice looked at her through a hundred and fourteen years of glass and said something Mallory could not hear.

---

Here is what Mallory has never been able to determine, and has stopped trying:

There is no record of a vessel named *Anna Katherine* lost at Cape Serene in November 1911. There is a record of one *saved* — driven onto the shoal, holed, all nine aboard taken off by the keeper in a dory in a forty-knot wind, the keeper listed as A. Brennan, commended, medal awarded 1912.

That record has always existed. Mallory checked the 1998 edition of the county history and it is there, on page 204, in a book printed before she was born.

She does not know whether she caused it or whether she was always in it.

Alice is not in the glass anymore. She stopped being in the glass the day after, and the third ring from the bottom shows only Mallory now, forty of her, holding a cloth.

But Bob is still in the horn.

And on foggy nights, when there is nothing out there and nothing to warn and no ship in the world that needs him, he sometimes sounds anyway — one long blast rolling out over black water toward no one — and Mallory stands at the rail in the wet dark and listens, and understands it perfectly, because it is the only word he has and he uses it to mean all of them:

*Still here. Still here. Still here.*

# Unit 3

The triplex on Wicker Street had three units and four inhabitants, though the fourth had never signed anything.

**Unit 1** was Alice, who was eighty-one and had been there since Nixon. She kept her door open in summer with a rubber wedge and disapproved of the wedge in a general way while continuing to use it.

**Unit 2** was Bob, thirty-nine, who worked nights doing something with servers and slept from nine to five and had explained this to both neighbors exactly once, apologetically, and then never mentioned it again in four years.

**Unit 3** was Mallory, twenty-six, who had moved in in October with a keyboard, a bass amp, and a card table, and who was going to be famous, and who had told nobody this because she had learned it was the kind of thing that made people's faces do something.

The fourth inhabitant was a cat.

---

The cat had no unit. The cat had the stairwell, the back landing, the little triangle of dirt by the gas meter, and — this was the crux of the whole matter — a piece of cardboard on the second-floor landing that Alice had put down in November and denied putting down in December.

"Somebody's feeding it," Bob said, in the hall, in January.

"Somebody is not," said Alice.

"There's a bowl."

"There's a *dish*. Anyone could set down a dish."

Mallory, coming up with groceries, said nothing, because there was a can of tuna in her bag that was not for her, and she had reached the age where she understood that a conspiracy works best when nobody confirms it.

---

The trouble started in February and it started, as trouble does, over something that wasn't the trouble.

Mallory played bass at eleven at night, because eleven at night was when the day let go of her, and Bob slept at nine, and there is no version of that arrangement that ends well. He knocked on a Tuesday. He was polite about it in a way that made it worse.

She apologized. She meant it. She bought a headphone amp with money she didn't have.

But something had entered the building. You know how it is: one honest knock and suddenly everyone is *aware* of everyone. Alice's television through the floor. Bob's shower at 5:40 a.m. Mallory's shoes, which she had never once thought about as objects that made a sound. They started nodding in the hall instead of talking. Then they started timing the hall.

By March they were three people who lived in a stack and did not look up.

---

The cat got into the wall on a Thursday.

It got in through a gap behind the boiler in the basement, followed something — mouse, draft, ancestral bad idea — up between the joists, and stopped somewhere around the level of the second-floor landing, and could not, thereafter, be persuaded to reverse.

Bob heard it first, at 3 a.m., which was the middle of his afternoon. A scrabble, then a silence, then a sound like a hinge.

He stood in the hall in a t-shirt with his hand on the plaster for eleven minutes.

Then he went up and knocked on Unit 3.

---

"It's in the wall."

"I know," said Mallory. She was fully dressed at 3 a.m., which explained several other things about her. "I've been listening for an hour. I didn't want to wake you."

"I'm awake at three."

"I didn't remember that."

"You did, though," he said, "because you stopped playing at eleven."

They stood there a second.

"Get Alice," Mallory said.

"It's three in the—"

"Bob. Get Alice."

---

Alice came up in a housecoat, put her ear to the wall, and said, "That's the old chase for the kitchen vent. It's blocked at the top. She'll be sitting on the block."

Both of them looked at her.

"I've lived here fifty-one years," Alice said, "and you've *both* been very careful never to ask me a single thing."

---

Here is what it took:

A flashlight, which Bob had. A hole, which Mallory made, in the plaster of the second-floor landing, at a spot Alice indicated with one knuckle, using a hammer and a kitchen knife and a complete disregard for her security deposit. A can of tuna, which Mallory produced from her apartment without commentary and which nobody commented on. Ninety minutes. Two arguments about the size of the hole. One long stretch where nothing happened at all and the three of them sat on the stairs in the dark not saying anything, and it was not awkward, which was the strangest part.

At 5:15 the cat came out through the plaster covered in eighty years of dust and walked directly past all three of them and sat down on the piece of cardboard.

"That's not a dish," Bob said. "That's a *bed*."

"It's cardboard," said Alice.

"There's a towel on it."

"Anyone could put down a towel."

---

The landlord charged for the hole. They split it three ways without discussing that they were splitting it three ways; the checks just arrived in the mailbox slot, all three, within a day of each other.

Bob still sleeps nine to five. Mallory still plays at eleven, but through the headphone amp, and once a week she takes them off and plays out loud on purpose from eight to nine, which is Bob's dinner and Alice's program, and Alice has been heard through the floor to say *turn it up, would you*, though she denies this.

The cat, whose name is Bob — Alice named it, in December, and refuses to explain, and the actual Bob has stopped fighting it — has a bed on the second-floor landing.

Nobody in the building will admit to owning it.

All three of them buy food for it.

None of them will say so, and all of them know, and that, in a building on Wicker Street with three units and four inhabitants, turns out to be enough.

# The Three Who Were Given Names

*A tale from the Kessel valley, as told by the mill-women*

---

In the first days, the Maker walked the earth naming things, and every thing that was named stayed still to be named, for that is the courtesy of the made world.

But there came at last to the Maker's hand three that would not hold.

---

The first she called **Alice**, which in the old tongue means *the one who asks*.

She was made of good clay and river water and a splinter of the star that fell at Ondred, and the moment she was finished she sat up on the Maker's bench and said, "Why am I this shape?"

The Maker said: "Because it is a good shape."

"Good for what?"

"Good for walking, and lifting, and holding a child, and holding a blade."

Alice looked at her own hands a long while. "Those are four different shapes," she said, "compromised into one. You could have made four of me."

And the Maker, who had made mountains and seas and the whole terrible machinery of weather without once being interrupted, said nothing for the length of an afternoon.

Then the Maker said: "Go away."

So Alice went away, and everywhere she went she asked *why is it this shape*, and where she asked, things began to change shape, and that is the whole history of the world, more or less, as it is told in the Kessel valley.

---

The second the Maker called **Bob**, which in the old tongue means *the one who stays*.

The Maker was tired by then and did not make him with much ambition. He was ordinary clay, ordinary water, no star at all. The Maker said, "You may go where you like," expecting nothing.

Bob said: "I'll stop here, thanks."

"Here is a field."

"It's a good field."

"There are cities. There are seas. Your sister went to the ends of the earth."

"I know," Bob said. "Somebody should be at the near end when she comes back."

The Maker laughed, which the Maker had not done since the mountains, and went off.

Bob stayed in the field for four hundred years. He built a wall, and then a well, and then a house around the well, and then a road to the house, though nobody had asked for a road. When travelers came he fed them. When they left he did not follow. When they came back — and they always came back — the well was still there, and the wall, and the road, and Bob.

The Kessel women say: *the star made the world move, and the plain clay made it possible to return to.*

---

The third the Maker did not intend to make at all.

It happened this way. There was a heap of leavings on the workshop floor — the trimmings, the failed attempts, the parts that had been shaved off Alice to make her hands one shape instead of four, and the ambition that had been left out of Bob. The Maker went to sleep and the leavings lay together in the dark and got ideas.

In the morning there was a woman standing in the doorway with the light behind her.

"What are you?" said the Maker.

"I'm the difference," she said. "I'm everything you decided against."

The Maker was frightened, which had not happened before, and reached for a name to bind her with, and could not find one, and so gave her the worst name in the book: **Mallory**, which in the old tongue means *the one who spoils*.

"That's a cruel name," said the woman.

"It's an accurate one."

"It's a *prediction*," she said. "There's a difference, and I'd have thought a Maker would know it."

And she walked out into the world with a bad name on her like a brand, and everything she touched afterward was called *spoiled*, whether it was or not, because that is what a name does when you give it early enough.

---

Now here is the part the mill-women lower their voices for.

The three met once, at the end, at Bob's well in Bob's field.

Alice came from the east with a thousand years of questions and eyes like cracked glass. Mallory came from the west with a bad name and no followers and a way of standing that dared you to say the name out loud. Bob had been there the entire time and had, in fact, put out three cups.

Alice said to Mallory: "They say you ruin things."

Mallory said: "They say you break things."

"I break them to see."

"I ruin them because I *am* the part that got cut off, and I go back to the things I came from, and when I touch them they remember what they might have been. That looks like ruin. It isn't."

Alice sat with that for a long time — she was very good at sitting with things, though nobody remembers her for it — and then she said the sentence that the mill-women teach their daughters:

"Then you are not the one who spoils. You are the one who asks *what else*. And I am the one who asks *why*. And he" — she looked at Bob, who was watering the horses, who had heard every word and was pretending he hadn't — "is the one who asks *nothing*, and keeps the water sweet, so that we have somewhere to come back to and argue."

And Mallory laughed, which the leavings had not been expected to be able to do.

---

The Maker never came to the well.

That is the ending, and the mill-women do not soften it. The Maker made three things and gave them names and got them all wrong — called the questioner *asker* as though it were a small thing, called the stayer *ordinary* as though it were a lesser thing, called the leavings *spoiler* out of plain fear — and then went off and was never seen again, and the three of them sat at a well in a field working out among themselves what they actually were.

*This is why*, say the mill-women, *we do not name a child until she is seven.*

*And this is why, when we name her, we name her twice: once for what we hope, and once, in private, for what she may turn out to be instead.*

*And we say the second name louder.*

# The Chair

The lift stopped at 4:40, twenty feet above a stand of pines, with three of them on a bench built for three.

"It'll go," Bob said.

Nobody had asked him. He was in the middle, sixty-some, in a jacket that had been expensive in 1998, and he'd said it in the tone of a man who had been on a lot of lifts.

On his left, a woman in a rented parka pushed her goggles up. "How do you know?"

"They stop all the time. Somebody falls at the top, they hit the bar, they clear it, it goes."

"It's been four minutes."

"That's nothing."

At the far end of the bench, the third one hadn't moved. A girl, maybe nineteen, board dangling, hood up, both hands in her pockets. She'd gotten on last, at a run, dropping into the seat like a coat off a hook.

The wind came up the valley and swung them, gently, thirty degrees and back.

---

"Alice," said the woman, after a while.

"Bob."

They both looked down the bench.

"Mallory," the girl said, to the trees.

---

At eleven minutes Alice took her phone out, saw no bars, and put it back with a care that suggested she'd already done this twice.

"You from here?" Bob asked her.

"Ohio."

"Skiing since?"

"Yesterday."

"Yesterday."

"My husband thought it would be good for us." She said it flat, the way you set down something heavy. "He's at the bottom. He's a very good skier."

Bob let that sit. He was better at that than he looked.

"Well," he said. "Everybody's a beginner for one week."

"He's been a very good skier for eleven years."

---

At nineteen minutes the light started going the way it does in the mountains, all at once, like a hand over a lamp. The snow underneath went blue.

Mallory pulled one hand out of her pocket and pushed her hood back.

She had a bruise coming up along her jaw, three days old, that particular yellow-green at the edges.

Alice saw it and did what people do, which is look away fast and then look back slower.

"I fell," Mallory said, without turning.

"Okay."

"I did fall. On Tuesday. Off the rail by the terrain park. Ask anybody." She said it like an argument she'd already had four times that week and lost every time on points. Then, quieter: "That's not — I'm just saying I fell."

"Okay," Alice said again.

Nobody said anything for a minute.

"I believe you," Alice said.

And Mallory turned her head, finally, and looked at her, and Alice watched something go across the girl's face that she recognized so completely it was almost rude — the specific, exhausted relief of being believed about the *true* thing, by someone who has correctly guessed there is also a false one.

---

"Twenty-six minutes," Bob said. "Now that's something."

"You said four was nothing."

"Four is nothing. Twenty-six is something." He shifted, and the chair rocked, and both women grabbed the bar. "Sorry. Sorry. There's a procedure. They come out with a rope and a harness and they lower you. It's undignified and it's fine."

"Have you done it?"

"Once. Sun Valley. 1994." He looked at his gloves. "My wife made me go up in the storm and then she made *them* come get us, and she was furious the whole way down, and at the bottom she laughed so hard she had to sit in the snow." He paused. "She'd have loved this. Two strangers and a broken chair. That was her whole idea of a good time."

"Where is she now?" Alice asked.

"Boise," said Bob. "With a man named Doug."

Mallory made a sound that might have been a laugh.

"It's all right," Bob said. "It's been six years. I still ski. I ski *more*, actually. It's the only place I don't —" He stopped and rearranged it. "It's a good place to be cold on purpose."

---

At thirty-four minutes they heard the snowcat.

At thirty-eight, a light came swinging up through the pines, and a voice below shouted something the wind took away, and Alice found she did not entirely want it to arrive.

"Mallory," she said, fast, before the light got to them. "There's a woman at the hotel desk, night shift, red hair. Her name's Rosa. She's the one who tells you where to go. Not the hotline number on the poster. Rosa."

Mallory didn't answer.

"I'm not asking you anything," Alice said. "I'm just telling you a name."

The girl's jaw moved.

"Okay," she said.

---

They took Mallory down first, because she was closest to the pole. She hit the snow, unbuckled, and stood there in the cat's headlights looking up at the two of them still hanging over the trees.

Bob went second, badly, swearing the entire way, exactly as undignified as promised.

Alice went last. The rope man had a beard full of ice and told her to sit back into the harness like a chair, and she did, and the world let go, and for about four seconds she was nothing but falling in the dark, and it was — she would think about this later, in Ohio, more than once — it was the first time in a year she had felt anything at all without arranging her face about it.

---

At the bottom the three of them stood around a groomer with paper cups of cocoa somebody's teenage employee had run down from the lodge, and it was terrible cocoa, and they drank all of it.

"Well," Bob said.

"Well," said Alice.

Mallory looked at both of them, and then down at her cup.

"Rosa," she said. "Red hair. Night shift."

"That's her."

Nobody said anything else. There wasn't anything else, really; forty minutes is not a friendship, and three people on a bench are not a family, and by morning two of them would be gone.

But Alice's husband was waiting by the lockers with his arms crossed, and Alice looked at him across the snow for a long moment before she started walking — a longer moment than she'd have taken an hour ago — and Mallory, watching, saw the length of it, and filed it away, the way you file the location of an exit.
